Steel Strike
2S7
On the Orders of the Day:

In the press of yesterday there appeared a despatch with regard to a steel strike at Sydney. I have information from the men that they applied for a board some weeks ago and were refused; that their members are being discriminated against because of their protest against a wage rate of 28 cents per hour, and that yesterday their active members were dismissed, the result being a spontaneous walk-out of workmen. Three thousand men are affected by this strike. Is it proposed that this board shall be granted? What further information can the government give us with regard to this industrial dispute?

Some four weeks ago the first information the Labour department had of a possible strike in the steel works at Sydney was in a newspaper item stating that a board was to be asked for to investigate the question of the adoption of the eight-hour day, the checkoff system, and an increase of 15 per cent in wages. The article stated that as the steel industry was not a public utility under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, a board would probably be denied by the Labour department. On the 31st day of January application for a board was made; it came to the Labour department on the third day of February. The workmen were advised at once that their application had been received and that we would ascertain from the officers of the British Empire Steel Corporation if they would be parties to the formation of a board. Yesterday the answer of the companies was received. It indicated the company would be unwilling to submit the question of the eight-hour day in the steel industry, to a board for investigation, as that matter had been dealt with in 1920 by a board, which unanimously indicated the belief that it would be impracticable to adopt an eight-hour day in the steel industry. The companies also stated that they would be unwilling to submit the question of the check-off system-which, in substance, means that the company would be required to collect the union dues of all workmen engaged in the steel plant-to a board, and that it would be inadvisable to submit to a board the question of an increase in wages, in view of the low price of steel products and the inability of the company, as it was stated, to make a profit instead of losses, wage increases were not possible. That information has been to-day conveyed to those who are now strikers at Sydney.
The information given the Labour department in regard to the actual strike is this: The day before yesterday an employee there, who thought he should be, for the time being, on account of the illness of a foreman, placed in the position of that foreman-threw some belts onto an idler, or in some other way interfered with the proper operation of the plant, and was promptly discharged therefor. The workers' union took the matter up and insisted on his immediate reinstatement, and when that was not granted they brought on a strike. The information received to-day is that the strike situation is serious indeed and that every effort is being made so to handicap the steel industry at Sydney as to cause- if they are successful in their undertakings- irreparable damage to the steel plant. I may say that is all the result of a campaign undertaken during the past few weeks in Sydney. For instance, I hold in my hand a newspaper containing a full-page advertisement; it is dated February third, but there were others in advance of this one. The advertisement reads:
Wanted!
1,000 Steel Workers Who Have Courage Not Fear
Who are Men, not Scabs Who will demand An Eight Hour Day,
15 per cent increase of Wages Recognition of the Union And Put it Through and Win a Victory Are you with us, or Against Us?
The strike appears to be a part of the campaign of the Workers' Party of Canada, which to all intents and purposes is the same as the Communist Party, or the party in control of affairs, it is said, in Russia at the present time. That is the cause of the trouble as it has developed, and I may say that we have to-day advised the strikers at Sydney that they should not interfere with the protection and maintainance of the plant to the extent of causing great damage to the property of the Steel Company. That is the situation, briefly, existing for the past few days.

That, in the opinion of this House, it is desirable that this government should create a commission for the purpose of making inquiry into the grain trade, whose findings might serve as a basis for improvement of present legislation relative thereto or for the creation |in the immediate future of some permanent solution of the grain marketing problem.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I realize in rising to make this motion that I am dealing with a matter of very great importance. First, Jet me say a few words in regard to the demand for a grain inquiry. There has been a persistent demand for it for some years,

Marketing of Grain
and committees have been appointed from time to time to try and find some better methods for marketing our grain, though it is true that a great many are under the impression that the present method, so far as its physical features are concerned, is as good as it is possible to get. During the last few months the farmers have met in con vention in the cities of Brandon and Saskatoon and passed resolutions in favour of a grain inquiry.
I should like to deal with a few matters in respect to which there is a general impression that there is a grievance, particularly on the part of the producer, but first a few words in regard to the methods by which we have advanced during the last twenty years. Many sitting in this House, and on this side particularly will remember the time when the conditions under which we marketed our grain were intolerable. I need not dwell on that; I merely wish to remind the House that it was a fact. Several times during the last two decades inquiries have been made, and I can think of no instance in which a thorough inquiry was made where it was not followed by legislation that has been of very great benefit to the producers and to the country as a whole. Commissions have been appointed in the province of Saskatchewan, and after one of these had completed its work and handed in its report, legislation was adopted providing for the creation of the Cooperative Elevator Company. I should like to contrast that procedure with the experience of the Manitoba government, which tried to apply legislative measures without first holding an inquiry. The question before them both was that of the government's owning and operating country elevators. In Saskatchewan, where they took the wise course of making an inquiry and careful investigation first, they have succeeded admirably, but in Manitoba, where they proceeded to apply legislative remedies without first holding an inquiry, they failed dismally. That .is so well known that I need not dwell upon it. In the year 1906 a commission was appointed and made a thorough investigation into the grain trade, and as a result of its inquiry proposed twenty-six changes. Twenty-four of these were accepted and approved and became part of the present Grain Act.
Some have asked, what results have followed these inquiries by commissions, and seem to be under the impression that an inquiry usually starts with nothing and ends with nothing. I have not time to dwell on all the improvements that have followed this particular investigation, but let me mention
only two which I think are well worthy of the consideration of the House. In the year 1907 and prior to that time, in the grain that was passing from Fort William to the transfer
elevators, there was an annual loss of 50,000 bushels. That had been going on for years. The lake carriers, when asked why they did not watch the scales to see they were not beaten out of their freights simply remarked, "The more you watch the elevator people the more they take from you, and we simply take our loss and add it to the cost of carrying.' The point I wish to make is this: After the remedial legislation recommended by the commission was applied, you will find if you look up the figures that after 1908 instead of there being a loss, the weights on the transfer elevators and at Fort William agreed very, very closely; in fact, there was practically no loss; and that has continued, I believe, up to the present time. I would ask if that is not a very definite and substantial benefit?-and it resulted from simply one suggestion from the grain commission.
Let me mention another. At that time it appeared as though there were abuses on the part of terminal elevators. It was very difficult to find out exactly what was taking place, but recommendations were made to remedy the abuses if they existed, and in the following year, 1909, or possibly 1910, several of the managers of the terminal elevators were prosecuted by the warehouse commission and fined S500 each on some five or six charges. That was another practical and helpful work of legislation resulting from a recommendation by one commission only. ] pass on. .
Some have raised this objection, that we expect that steps will be taken to create a wheat board. I am in sympathy with that idea; in fact, I propose to urge the creation of a wheat board. But the faults of which I am going to speak nearly all existed under the wheat board of 1919, and I cannot see that they would not continue to exist under a new wheat board. What are they? The spread in the country elevator between the track price and the street price is very great. Now I would like it to.be understood that the amount of grain handled in the country elevators is so small that they cannot make both ends meet-that is, the country elevators by themselves, receiving only the handling charges, are not paying propositions. And it is alleged-I will not say the allegations are all true-and our people generally believe, that a large part of this loss is made up by taking a too heavy toll from the man who is compelled to sell

Marketing oj Grain

his grain on the street. That man has not a carload, therefore he is at the mercy of the elevator. That is one allegation that is made and one which, I think, should be investigated by this inquiry board.
Another matter is this. An organization of grain buyers in the West are making very serious charges against the grain trade. I do not assume the responsibility for their statements, I do not know that the charges are all true; but they are very serious in character. They claim that those who employ them, the firms in Winnipeg, are using very strong pressure, amounting to intimidation and even threats, in order to induce them to take a greater toll from the farmers than they have any right to do. They are bonded to become good-that is what it practically amounts to-for any shortage. Their contention is that though they have purchased grain for a firm for many years they are not permitted by the firms for whom they purchase to know the outturns of the cars as they go to Fort William. The grain firms follow this practice: If a buyer writes to Fort William and asks for the outturns of its cars they are at once notified by the chief weigh-master and the grain firms thwart the buyers. This is their contention. The grain firms rather reproach the buyers when they ask for these outturns. They tell them, "We would supply them to you if you ask for them"; but the buyers allege that they have not been able to get these statements in a satisfactory manner from the firms who employ them. They are kept in the dark as to whether they are going to be short or not, and at the same time they are bonded to become responsible for any shortage. This keeps them in the position where they are constantly striving to get all the grain they can lest there should be a shortage for which they would be held responsible.
The buyers also allege that the bonding firms are in collusion with the grain firms to intimidate them and keep them in subjection; giving them anything but a square deal. Now it may be that they have tried to have these matters investigated by the Board of Grain Commissioners, and it may be that there is not much foundation for their charges, but it seems to me it is only fair that some regard should be paid to the wishes of a body of men-I do not suppose all are members of this organization-whose membership runs into many hundreds. They are the men to whom we must sell our grain, it must pass through their hands before it goes on to Fort William, and it seems to me that in view of the fact that they have been making these charges openly-in a little pamphlet

they have issued, on the platform, and in every conceivable way they can get the charges before the public-it seems to me only reasonable that opportunity should be given to prove whether these charges are true or false.
Since this resolution was placed on the order paper, a select committee of this House has been appointed, and it may be the opinion of some that this committee could successfully inquire into all these matters. I would submit, however, that the charges I have just mentioned could not possibly be inquired into by this committee, for the reason that the organization referred to would probably make charges against a dozen, possibly two dozen, grain firms in the city of Winnipeg. It would be unfair to allow7 such charges to be preferred without giving the grain firms the oportunity of defending themselves. That would mean summoning witnesses by the score, it would mean occupying a great length of time, and it would be a very expensive process, because many of these witnesses live out in the country and probably would not be in a position to leave their work and spend a week or ten days in the city of Ottawa. Moreover the programme allotted to the select committee in question is so large and comprehensive that no committee, in the given time, could possibly cover one-quarter of the work laid out for it. That is quite evident and I need not labour the point. We all know how long it took the Committee on Agriculture to deal with the wheat board question last session- it occupied somewhere about three months' time. Now the work laid out for this select committee will probably cover four or five times as much ground. In that event, how is it possible for the committee to do justice to more than a very small part of the programme referred to it?
It has also been urged that the present Board of Grain Commissioners have the power, and it is their duty, to investigate these charges-that if anything wrong has occurred it is within the jurisdiction of the grain commission to investigate it. Let me point out the position in which the grain commissioners would find themselves if that course were pursued. Suppose a charge of injustice or irregularity in connection with a terminal elevator, or a country elevator for that matter, were made. These institutions are run under regulations laid down by the Board of Grain Commissioners, and the commissioners would be in the position of sitting in judgment of their own acts. Therefore, I submit, the Board of Grain Commissioners are not the proper authorities to investigate

Marketing of Grain
these charges. Furthermore I am going to ask, among other things, that some changes be made in the Grain Act. Now I cannot conceive that the board would seriously regard it as a part of their duty to submit such changes in the Grain Act, although they might. I think they have known in the past that charges of injustice in connection with the inspection of grain have been made, and yet no recommendation, so far as I know, has come from that board. I had occasion to write to the grain commission some little time ago when the grain firms were following this course in connection with cheques issued for purchases of grain: They sent cheques to the farmers for the cars they had purchased and put the necessary stamps on the cheques all right, but they charged the farmers for the stamps. I wrote to the grain commission and pointed out that fact, but they took the stand that the matter was not within their jurisdiction. Now, if they regard little matters of that nature as not being within their jurisdiction, and if complaints have been made and have failed of investigation by the commission and no remedies are forthcoming, what is the use of going on year after year and waiting for a remedy which fails to appear? We cannot get a remedy for the difficulties which exist and yet plenty of time has been allowed to provide a remedy. Under the circumstances the time has come to adopt a better means of securing redress.
I have touched on the matter of the inspection of grain. Let me deal a little more in detail with that point. At the present time it is believed-it is not my opinion only but it is the general belief-by the producers of grain that they are not securing a just return for wheat of a certain nature, The wheat that I refer to is of this character: grain that has been damaged slightly, or at least slightly discoloured by rain. Nothing but the milling test will determine whether the grain has been damaged. Much of that grain is being graded as No. 3 Northern. Milling tests have been made again and again. A firm in Minneapolis made one test some years ago; our provincial governments have made tests; tests have been made in the city of Winnipeg; and in all cases it has been found that many of those samples of grain from No. 3 Northern, of the kind of which I speak, have proved to be equal in milling value to our very best No. 1. Northern. That has been proved beyond r, doubt. The difficulty is how to classify this grain so that it shall be sold for its proper value. Some years ago a suggestion was made from the grain trade, and for a time was
19*
backed up by a few farmers, in favour of creating a sample market, in order that this grain might be sold on sample. In a very short time, the farmers, looking into the matter, began to see that it was not in their interest. It simply meant that the best of each grade, the choice cars, would be picked out, and the poor cars would be allowed to go forward, and would be the basis of the price fixed on the Liverpool market. It would be a skimming off of the cream, and allowing the skimmed milk to go forward. The farmers at once commenced opposition to the creation of a sample market. That opposition has continued up to the present time, notwithstanding the fact that the sample market was created some years ago. Let me point out to hon. members that although that sample market has been in existence for some years, very few bushels, if any, have ever passed over the sample market, but with the sample market went the mixing privileges 

an excuse and a reason for the existence of the mixing elevator. I think I am not unfair or unjust when I say that those who asked for the sample market did not want the sample market, but wanted the mixing privileges. I am not prepared to say definitely how that grain can be classified. I will add a little more to the class I have just spoken of: It is not only grain that has been slightly bleached by being wet, but also grain that has been slightly frosted. There is in some years a considerable quantity of grain of that nature, and the farmers who raised it are selling it sometimes for fifteen and sixteen cents a bushel less than No. 1 Northern, whereas, it has been proved beyond a doubt that it is of as much value and as good milling wheat as No. 1 Northern. That, I claim, is a very great injustice, and I believe a change should be made in the Inspection Act, but I am not prepared to say just what it should be. If I could tell you exactly how that could be remedied, I do not know that there would be very much reason why a grain commission should investigate it. That is a matter which could and should be dealt with by a select committee, although I have pointed out some matters that could not be dealt with by them.
There is another evil to which I will refer. I suppose some of you would find it hard to believe, but there has been a practice in the past of substituting cars. Cars that
4	p.m. are near the top of the grade are of excellent quality, and those mixing elevators would want them very much, though by some mysterious method the cars have been selected from the general flow of grain and have been sent to the mixing elevators, and

Marketing of Grain
cars of poorer quality have been put in their places. This, at one time, was carried on on a very large scale. There is a very great injustice. As I have pointed out-and I think I shall repeat because I want hon. members to appreciate the point-the price that the farmer receives for his grain is based on the kind of grain and on the value of the grain as it arrives in the Old Country market, and when the grain is deteriorated, damaged in any way, and the value taken out of it, then the price is less, and the farmer must suffer the loss. Sometimes, when a commission of inquiry engages in this work it will find evils of which nothing was known previously. I remember one remarkable case of this sort-it is quite possible that something of that nature might be discovered, if a board of inquiry were appointed at the present time. Investigation took place in Minneapolis some year or more ago, in which it was found that scalping played a very large part. That is, a grain firm would buy from a farmer and they would transfer to another grain firm. Sometimes, it would be a legitimate transaction and sometimes it would not. In some cases, carloads of grain were sold five or six or seven or eight times, and the spread between the first and second selling price was sometimes thirty and forty cents a bushel. Now as a great many grain firms that are doing business in Minneapolis are also doing business in Fort William, the relations between the two exchanges are very close, and the practice followed in the two exchanges is veiy much alike. I have no knowledge that the evil practice of scalping is carried on on a large scale, or to any great extent, in Fort William, or rather in Winnipeg, but the fact is that it is .a growing evil, and as the commission denounced it roundly in Minneapolis, it would seem to me to be a question that the board of inquiry might investigate carefully.
Let me touch very briefly on a matter I think of considerable importance. Under the wheat board, I think it is common knowledge among farmers that the spread between No. 1 Northern and No. 3 Northern is seven cents- it stood at seven cents during the whole season. Wheat, you will notice, was nearly $3 a bushel. Now, mark you, after the wheat board ceased operations and the price of wheat dropped to about $1.50 a bushel, the spread, instead of being one half of seven cents, was doubled; instead of being 3J cents, the spread increased to fourteen cents and in some cases to fifteen cents. It does not matter very much to a man who is growing No. 3 Northern wheat if the price of No. 1 Hard or No. 1 Northern is good, so long as he has not

that kind of wheat, but what is a serious matter to him is the fact, if he has No. 3 Northern wheat, that the spread between No. 1 Northern and No. 3 Northern is sixteen cents, and it brings him a very small price, indeed. Can anyone well explain that? Is it not worthy of some investigation by a board of inquiry, that the spread between No. 1 Northern and No. 3 Northern was seven cents and since the wheat board went out of business, [DOT] the spread doubled, notwithstanding that the price of wheat went down? I think it well worthy of consideration.
Let me say a word in regard to mixing elevators. A few years ago there were very few mixing elevators, Now there are a great many; and I suppose the reason is quite evident-they are profitable. Grain is taken into the mixing elevators, and according to the regulations of the Board of Grain Commissioners, as it is inspected out, it should grade up to the average. But what takes place in the meantime? Nos. 3, 4, 5-we do not know what grades, sometimes it is one and sometimes another-are mixed together and as the grain goes out of the elevators the lower grades disappear entirely. What has happened is this. They have cleaned the good grain out of the lower grades; their weights increase; a great deal of the poorer grain in the lower grades has gone out as screenings and a considerable quantity of the better grain has been mixed in, so that wheat that has gone in as No. 6, or No. 5 or No. 4 may go out as No. 2 or No.
3.	A strong argument is advanced by the trade that this is really a benefit to the farmer, that it does him no harm but rather improves some of his grain, and that not so much storage is required. I grant you the last point, but I deny the others. I think that this practice entails a great loss to the producer of grain. In the first place, if the good cars are taken out of the general flow, what happens to the rest? The question arises, is the grain which goes out of the mixing elevators up to the average required by the regulations? I would not say that it is not, at the present time, because I believe that the change in the personnel of the Board of Grain Commissioners has very greatly improved the board. But I would point out that within the last few months, at least within the last year, one cargo went to the United States graded out of one of these elevators as "3 Northern straight." When it got to Buffalo it was held up, the purchaser refused to accept it, the inspectors drew samples which were sent back to Winnipeg, and it was declared by them that the grain instead of being "3 Northern

Marketing oj Grain
straight" was "3 and 4 tough." I know that that is only a matter of administration, and it is quite possible that it calls for no change in the regulations, but I think a board of inquiry would not do any harm if it investigated that matter along with others. How was it that a similar cargo was sent to the Old Country and there found in the same condition and rejected? I would mention another point in connection with these mixing elevators. In the evidence taken by the Committee on Agriculture last year, it was pointed out that there was considerable difficulty in getting rid of the grain. I do not know just where this happened, but the fact is that when James Stewart was head of the wheat board he refused to take grain out of these mixing elevators except at a discount of as high as four cents per bushel. What does it indicate, when a man who was competent and knew the grain trade thoroughly, refused to take grain out of the mixing elevators except at such a discount? It is pointed out, of course, that he did not exercise his powers in this matter. But what do we infer from that? Knowing whom they had to deal with and that he would take his discount if the grain was not up to the mark, they sent it out at the right grade. But in the past it has not always been that way. Now, even supposing that the grain goes out of the mixing elevators up to the average, the value for mixing purposes that is in the grain as it passes from the producers' wagons is taken out. I believe that the Old Country importer and miller, knowing that they buy our grain not for its intrinsic value as milling grain, but for its strength for mixing purposes, would use that grain for those purposes themselves, and if they got it unadulterated I think they would pay a higher price for it than they give at present. If that be true-and I think the point is well worth looking into-then the farmer is being robbed of something to which he has a right, because he is entitled to the full value of his grain as it passes from his wagon. Anything that damages grain or takes from its value in transit takes from it something to which the farmer is entitled. It has been told me, and the statement has been made on such good authority that I have no hesitation in repeating it, that a considerable quantity of grain is transferred between the mixing and the public elevators. For what purpose is this done? It is alleged that these mixing elevators have difficulty in getting rid of their grain, and the millers admitted in evidence last session before the agricultural committee that they would never take grain from the mixing elevators if they could possibly help it. That was their evidence, one and all. Now, when they have that difficulty in getting rid of their grain what do they do? It is stated that they send it to the public elevators. It then passes into the general bin. If it is not up to mark, or if the value has been in any way impaired, it passes to the general bin and goes to lessen the value of the grain that is shipped to the Old Country, and on which the price is based.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext: Does my hon. friend intend to imply that the public elevators are doing the mixing at the head of the lakes?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext: No, not necessarily so. The grain that has been mixed and skimmed down as low as the inspection system would permit, to such an extent that the millers do not want it, the exporters do not want it, and James Stewart will not take it except at a discount, is sent over to the public elevators where it loses its identity and becomes straight grade grain.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext: But my hon. friend says that it was put into the general bins and thereby impaired the standard of the grain already there. Is not that mixing, and is it not contrary to law?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
What I am pointing out is that whatever value that grain would have for blending purposes, if it were not mixed, is thereby lost. That is to say, if that grain were sent over to the Old Country unmixed it would have a value - for mixing purposes which it loses when mixed in the mixing elevators.
Now, some time ago a statement appeared in a great many of our newspapers that must have cost a considerable amount of money. It was published by the secretary of the Grain Exchange, Dr. Magill, and appeared in many of the agricultural papers and the daily papers all over the country. We know that this advertising is quite expensive, and that statement must have cost a good deal. In it, it is claimed by Dr. Magill that all that the trade at Winnipeg takes out of a bushel of wheat is 4.3 cents. Now, anyone who knows anything about grain, anyone who knows the number of people that are employed on the exchange, the profits they are evidently making, the staffs they keep, the enormous army that feed off the handling of the grain, will know quite well that these people could not live very long if that were all they got from the grain. If 4.3 cents per bushel were all they got I think some of them would starve inside of six months. It is quite evident that there are underground ways of reaping a greater profit from the
Marketing of Grain

grain than that. It is obvious that this is not all the profit they receive. And that is one reason why, it seems to me, a commission should be appointed, not to look into any one of these charges, but to go into the whole subject from every point of view. All the circumstances taken together constitute a sufficient ground for the appointment of a commission to inquire into the matter.
There is another point I should like to mention. I know representatives of the trade on the Liverpool and London markets are very anxious to know just what steps are taken by the Canadian government to see that no deterioration of our grain takes place between Fort William and the seaboard. They ask again and again:	Inspection takes place
at Fort William; what inspection takes place after that? The grain is handled through elevators, some of which are private elevators. Are the steps that are taken to safeguard the various grades of grain sufficient and adequate? I know quite well that such steps in regard to grain that passes through American channels are not sufficient. I found on the other side of the water a great many complaints about grain that had come from American ports, and the trade could not understand why it was that such grain was not as good as that coming from Fort William. Although the evidence was not given on oath, it was discovered either at New York or Boston that after the grain passing through the American channels in bond has left the seaboard, it is considered to be out of bend and the grades are then mixed. Here I believe is a very strong reason why there should be an investigation into the trade, because 65 per cent of our grain is now passing through American channels. Our railways are crying out for more freight, and our elevators at Montreal, although they had all they could do last year, I am sure would not admit that they could not do more business. We want our trade kept in Canadian channels, and I believe that an inquiry might do much to this end, because the variation of a single cent in carriage would mean a great deal; it would keep millions of bushels in Canadian channels that are now passing out through American channels.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext: Before the hon. member leaves that subject, has he figures as to how much American grain passed through Canadian channels in the same period?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
I could not give exact figures to the hon. member. I know the amount is considerable. I suppose some people migh take the attitude that while as much American grain passes through Canadian channels

as Canadian grain passes through American channels, why, we are enjoying a square deal and have nothing to complain of. I do not take that view. It seems to me that the Americans take all they can get, and they would not stop if they got more than their share. And we too should get all we can. I do not think the Americans would blame us.
I am not just certain whether another matter should be brought under this inquiry, but I think it would do no harm if the possibilities of creating co-operative systems for handling our farm products were investigated and reported on,. This system has been adopted in the United States with considerable success, especially by the fruit growers, and a little more information on the subject to our farmers that would eventually help them to solve their marketing problem by the creation of such a system would be of great value. It is well known that the wheat board which we are asking for and expecting this year is only regarded as a temporary expedient. We are looking for something that is permanent. We have not yet found it. It might be possible that a grain inquiry would serve as a kind of cleansing of our present system and wipe out some of those evils or clear up misapprehension. If so, our people might be satisfied to continue the same system, but I doubt it very much. Otherwise we want some other system of handling our grain, and it is the general belief that the co-operative system will be found the best. Any assistance that could be given by this board of inquiry would be very much appreciated by the farmers.
In closing, I am going to make one suggestion. Commissioners have gone to the Old Country and investigated the condition in which grain arrives there. There has been a strong feeling on the part of some that grain arrives very much deteriorated; in fact, extreme statements have sometimes been made to the effect that the grain reaches there as chicken feed. That has never been anywhere nearly true. But unfortunately those commissioners that have been sent to the Old Country have not numbered among them a single grain inspector, and I believe the government will be well advised to send a well qualified grain inspector overseas to look into this matter and to report back to the grain commission and to the inspection department the actual condition in which grain is arriving there, and also to make suggestions for overcoming any trouble that his investigations may disclose. A great deal could be accomplished by getting in touch with the trade there and encouraging them to further develop business with the

Marketing of Grain
Canadian people. If a competent inspector were kept there for six months or possibly a year I believe it would be money well spent.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext: Why not permanently?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
The member for Saltcoats asks, why not' permanently? Well, that is a matter for future consideration. After a period of one year, if it were found advisable to keep such an official there, I certainly would have no objection to his being retained.
You will note, Sir, that I have not dwelt to any great extent on the serious conditions prevailing among the producers of grain, but this is simply because I think those conditions have been mentioned often enough by others. I think the House appreciates the fact that it would be a very great inspiration and help if something were done to give those producers encouragement, before they sell their next crop, that something of a practical nature is being done to relieve the difficulties under which they labour. Because, we must continue to sell our grain in competition with the other countries of the world, and accept prices regulated by supply and demand, while, as has been many times said, we are compelled to buy in very, very high markets. On these grounds I ask hon. members to support this resolution.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext: I should like to ask the hon. member a couple of questions. He has mentioned a sample market. Does he favour the operation of a sample market? The other question is in regard to deterioration. He referred to the deterioration of grain going from the head of the lakes or Winnipeg to the London or Liverpool market and the interest that the farmer had in that grain. Is it not true of a very large proportion of the wheat sold by the farmer at the track, that once he delivers it to the country elevator his interest in that wheat ceases entirely? I am asking for information in both these cases.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
I will answer the last question first, lest I forget it. That ground has often been taken, that as soon as a farmer sells his load of grain at the country elevator, and receives his price therefor, he has absolutely no further interest in that grain. I think that is what my hon. friend means. But that is not so in any case, not even as to a part of his crop. The price he receives for that- load has been based on the actual value of grain arriving in the Old Country. That is, those who are importing the grain know what they have been receiving for that grade. It does not matter what the grade is, but we will say it is No. 3; they know what they have been receiving for No.
3 in the past, and if anything is done in transit to lower the value of that grain, the price will be less. It is plain that if the price is less the price to the farmer will be less; there is no getting away from that. So that the farmer is interested in what happens to that grain from the time it leaves his wagon until it is sold to the Old Country buyer.
The question has been raised with regard to a sample market. When a very considerable part of our grain is milled in Canada, I shall be in favour of a sample market, but so long as nearly all our grain is sold by grade, I cannot see my way clear to favour a sample market. What takes place is simply this-and I do not know that I need cover the ground; in fact, I believe I have already done so-it is a picking out of the best cars, the cars that are of great value, and getting them for the same price as for the ordinary cars; little or no premium is paid. What is left is less valuable, but it is on what is left that the price is based; therefore the price is less.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. "Speaker, I rise to support this resolution; I believe that an investigation into the grain trade is long overdue. The world's price for wheat is set at Liverpool, because Liverpool, being the great centre for wheat, collects the surplus practically of the whole world. It is this surplus, or the lack of any surplus at all, that sets the price for wheat all over the world. We, the growers in western Canada, are content if we get that- price, minus the cost of getting our surplus on that market.
The farmer can market his grain in one of several different ways. He can sell outright to a country elevator at a price based on the Winnipeg price-to a dealer whose interest it is to create as much difference as possible between the initial price and the price paid at Winnipeg. Now, the farmer may possibly load a car over the loading platform and ship to Fort William and Port Arthur, in which case he will save the spread that may exist between the elevator prices and the cash prices in Winnipeg, as well as avoid the effects of all the devious methods of elevator operators regarding grades, shrinkage, dockage, and so on. He may send his car down to be stored at the terminal elevator, and to be sold later when the price suits him, in which case he is given a certificate guaranteeing the weight and grade. But that car of wheat may be spotted on the way by some miller and diverted to his mill for his own use, or it
Marketing oj Grain

may be diverted to a private elevator for mixing purposes; and all the farmer has to show for it is a certificate. If his car is diverted, it means that the wheat was a particularly fine type of that grade, and it also means, that, although the price is made in Liverpool, according to the value the British miller sets on Canadian wheat in competition with the wheat of other countries, the British miller does not get a chance at the wheat as it leaves the farmer's wagon. I think it should be made illegal for anyone to go into the business of buying and selling with no intention of ever taking possession or delivering in case of sale. Many of these men at one time or another overstep their capabilities and have to unload in a hurry. When they do this, advantage is taken of it by the exporter; the price is beaten down, and that sets a price for the next twenty-four hours over the whole of the three prairie provinces. It is possible, too, for a combination of these men, by withholding or dumping, to influence the price the way they want it. It is unfair, I say, to the grower that the remuneration for his year's work should be subject to such haphazard methods of price fixing and resulting violent fluctuations-seeing that he has no other channel open to him through which he can market his wheat.
While I believe in as little government control of industry in any form as possible, one must realize that wheat is different from all other commodities in that, because of its great bulk it must be moved from the grower to the consumer 'in a collective way. The grower has no control over any part of the business after the wheat leaves the wagons at the initial loading point, and yet his price is subject to the speculation of a set of men who are interested only in making all the difference they can between the price at the initial point and the Liverpool market. Since the farmer's price is established outside of his province, outside of his country, in competition with the wheat of other countries, it is surely the duty of the government to see that the grower is protected to the point where his product cannot be further tampered with, either in the physical handling or in the matter of price fixing. Since this product of the farmer is one which must be handled collectively and which has to pass through thj hands of so many public utilities before it reaches the place where the price is set, I say again it is the duty of this government so to regulate these public utilities as to guarantee that full justice shall be done to those who are particularly interested in such products.

Many features of the trade which this commission should investigate are outside the province of the present grain commission. I think it is necessary that some consideration should be given by the commission of inquiry to the routes by which the grain of this country can reach its ultimate destination in the most economical way. I shall hope to see the appointment of men in this capacity who, by their integrity and ability, will command the respect of all concerned.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
I rise to associate myself with the sentiments expressed by the two former speakers concerning this resolution. It is a cause of gratification to me that the government has so far conceded the point as to have this problem investigated by the select Committee on Agriculture, for a problem it is, and it has been a problem in the West ever since the West has been growing grain. I do not, however, think that the committee will have either the time or the opportunity to take all the evidence that is necessary in this matter. By way of illustration let me say that when a committee of this House sits and takes evidence it is only natural, and it is what we have been accustomed to find in the past, that the financial interests in the country, particularly those engaged in the grain trade, always send their delegations to give evidence before the committee, and invariably they are composed of capable men who give expert evidence. But I maintain that the producer, the man whose cause has been pleaded here to-day, and whose cause I am now endeavouring to plead, has not the same opportunity of giving evidence before a committee of this House that he would have before a royal commission, and that is one reason why I rise to make a small contribution to this debate.
I should like to see a royal commission appointed that would travel all over the country and give the producer, the man who has a grievance, and who has always had one -the man who is not receiving justice, and particularly so this last year-an opportunity to appear before it and give evidence. In my humble opinion that is necessary before justice can be done; but as I said before, I am pleased that the government have conceded the point of appointing a committee at all events. I hope that if the committee has not finished its work by the end of the session, and that if its work warrants continued investigation, as I think it will, the government will appoint a royal commission that will travel over the country and give all parties concerned an opportunity to give their

Marketing of Grain
evidence, and then bring in their report which the government might act upon through order in council so that it would not be necessary to wait until another session was called, but give relief before the next crop was marketed.
The two speakers who have preceded me have entered into quite a technical point. For myself I wish to give only concrete evidence.
I believe the commission could and would find out the conditions if they would only travel over the country and give the producer an opportunity to present his evidence. I might state that I think I have a right to speak for the producer, because I have endeavoured to take a man's part in the harvesting of thirty-one crops in that western country, and surely if an individual has done that much work, he should know something whereof he speaks and of the conditions surrounding the producing of grain.
As the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) said, the spread between the price the producer receives and the price that is received on the market at Liverpool is altogether too great, and in the first place it is the producer of the grain who pays all the charges between, to say nothing of the inequalities of which the hon. gentleman speaks.
We have heard the complaint of the miller, and in my humble opinion the eastern miller, in the province of Ontario, we will say, is warranted in complaining on the ground that the grain which he buys to grist in his mill has lost much of its value because of its being purchased at the mixing elevators. The grain he gets is not as a rule of the same quality as the grain forwarded to the initial elevators by the producer, and that difference in price is always deducted from the producer. I have no doubt it may seem that this point has always been stressed in the House, but it has not been stressed very much until the last three or four years, and that is one of the reasons why men are down here now endeavouring to bring the matter before the House. I think I can assure the House that when the conditions are recognized and remedies applied, you will not have the same complaint from the people of the West. It is simply because remedies have not heretofore been applied that we are obliged to come here and ask for redress for our grievances.
I stated a few moments ago that I pro-, posed to present some real concrete evidence, something of which I am absolutely certain. I would call the attention of the House to the fact that in the year 1920 I made a statement on the floor here to the effect that I had visited the state of North Dakota and
had found a great disparity in the price paid there to the man who sold his grain to the initial elevator and the price paid to his neighbour just north of an imaginary boundary line. I found a difference of $1.01 a bushel between the price paid to the Dakota farmer and the price paid to the farmer in the West. In this country we had a wheat board in existence at that time and over there there was none. The explanation given by the interests-naturally it does not come from the producer, yet it is the producer on our side who suffers and has suffered for years- was that the United States required what hard wheat could be taken across the boundary for the purpose of mixing at the Minneapolis mills to provide a grade of flour acceptable to the consumer in the British Isles. That is true, and all very well, but. we find to-day that the United States is scarcely an exporting country; in fact, we believe that in the very near future she will forego the large revenue she has derived in the past from the export of flour; yet this same condition exists today. Again this year, for my own satisfaction and for the purpose of being in a position to furnish evidence to the House or before a committee, I made another visit to the state of North Dakota, and on the day of my arrival, which was 9th October, I found a spread of 11 cents a bushel between the price paid the North Dakota producer and the price paid north of the boundary line, and that was for a poorer grade of wheat than ours. They were receiving 93 cents a bushel, while I was receiving only 82 cents. I make this positive statement. In my judgment, and from what knowledge I have gained in seeing samples of grain, my grain that I sold this year-and you will pardon the personal pronoun, but I can speak more positively of my own case-was fully two grades better than the grain over in the elevators that I visited in the town of Sherwood in North Dakota; yet my neighbour was getting 93 cents a bushel while I received only 82 cents. When I reached home I found in my mail a map sent by the Railway Association of Canada, which shows the 49th parallel and the lines of railway paralleling the international boundary line. It also shows the comparative freight rates from points opposite each other along the international boundary, and I find that in each case there is a difference of 4| cents per one hundred pounds in favour of Canada. We might call that equal to 2 6/10 cents a bushel. Add that to the 11 cents premium that my neighbour to the south was receiving, and for a poorer grade of wheat. I went home quite prepared to ask this further question,-why is it, when

Marketing oj Grain
Liverpool is the pivotal point where the price is fixed for all export wheat, that my neighbour to the south of the boundary can receive 11 cents more than I, and all these other favourable conditions? It does seem to me, and I urge it upon the House, that this is one of the questions which the commission should investigate and determine.
I also submit that a committee of this House could not secure the necessary evidence. It would be different with a royal commission moving through the country and hearing evidence at various points. I am sure in that case the producers of grain would only be too anxious, oniy too glad, to have the opportunity of appearing before them and giving concrete evidence upon the points referred to. The evils in connection with this matter have been apparent for many years, and it is a cause of gratification to us today, Sir, to know that our government have recognized the fact and are adopting means whereby we hope to obtain redress. It has been a subject of complaint in the past that governments have been loath to take action in the matter; I am happy to think that a change for the better has taken place in that respect.
It occurred to me, when the hon. member for Qu'Appelle suggested that an officer should be located in the Old Country to look after our grains, preferably at Liverpool, that our government might have obtained samples from the Liverpool market and laid them before the members of this House, or at least before the Committee on Agriculture which is to look into this matter. I might state that as a producer I am prepared to collect samples of grain as grown in the prairie provinces in the year 1922, and I am prepared to establish the grades upon which the producer was paid; it would be a very nice comparison for individual members of this House to see the quality of grain that was produced and sold last year as against the quality of grades that are fixed as standards upon the Liverpool market.
May I give another concrete instance illustrating the conditions that prevailed in 1922. I read in the statutes that:
No. 1 Northern grain shall be sound and well cleaned, weighing not less than 60 pounds to the bushel, and ' shall be composed of at least 60 per cent hard wheat. No. 2 Northern shall be sound and reasonably clean, of good nulling quality, 58 pounds to the bushel, 45 per cent hard wheat.
The illustration that I wish to give the House, and I hope it will come before the committee, was furnished by an individual whose entire grain crop was grown upon prairie land that was newly broken. This individual purchased really good Marquis seed 	;
wheat from a responsible seed firm, and it was sown upon this land. I myself saw this crop many times, and helped to thresh and market the grain. When that grain was being marketed by the load on the street all the buyers were very anxious to purchase it, in all cases at the maximum price of No. 1 Northern. The producer placed 1,206 bushels of this wheat in the elevator to ship out, and when it was shipped out he received the grade of No. 2 Northern. Complaint was made and a re-inspection asked for, but the reply the producer received was, "We are not paying No. 1 Northern prices for wheat this year." Now I am prepared to take my oath, Sir, that that grain weighed 62 pounds to the bushel, that it contained more than 80 per cent hard wheat, and that it was as beautiful a hard, red wheat as anyone would wish to see. Yet that was the treatment accorded to that fine grain. I have wondered many times how many cars of a poorer grade of wheat those 1,206 bushels were intended to be mixed with to conform to the standard of grade required on the Liverpool market. That illustrates the problem which confronts the producers to-day, and it is an injustice to refuse them the opportunity of appearing before a commission.
Eeferring again to the question of the spread in prices in the state of North Dakota I wish to state that since the date to which I referred previously the spread there has gone up to as much as 21 cents per bushel, and the question arises why it is that a grower in the United States who produces wheat under the same conditions and suffers the same disability that I do, should receive 21 cents per bushel more for an inferior grade when the price for export wheat is set at the pivotal point of Liverpool. That is a very important question and one which enters largely into the question of immigration, as I would remind my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Stewart). How largely it affects the question of immigration I can best demonstrate by citing a newspaper quotation which I would like to have placed upon Hansard. It reads thus:
On Wednesday, December 13th, the Whitehead family, comprising Mrs. Whitehead, Sr., Mrs. Wm. Whitehead, Jr., and Edmund took their departure from this district proceeding to Sherwood en route for Michigan. This is the fourteenth family to leave this locality with no one up to the present coming to take their places. Out of the number gone only one was a bachelor.
That is the condition which prevails in the West; it is the condition which prevails all along the international boundary. And again I state, and reiterate, that this matter is one which we must take into considera-

Marketing oj Grain
tion, because there must be an equitable price paid to those who are producing grain and who are working fourteen and fifteen hours a day in so doing. I say that the question of immigration does enter into this matter and that the exodus from western Canada must be stopped. Because there should be the fullest opportunity of demonstrating what the West is worth. The potential wealth of the country is not challenged, the people of the West have a heritage that is well worth while; but parasites must be stopped from stepping in and taking an unjust toll from the people who are labouring there.
I am very pleased indeed that the government have at last made a move towards investigating the conditions about which we have for so long complained.
Mr. ARTHUR L. BEAUBIEN (Proven-cher):	Mr. Speaker, when coming down to
Ottawa last year, a large percentage of the electors of Provencher, which I have the honour to represent here, told me that they thought that a royal commission to inquire into the grain trade should have been established long ago. I thought so myself and was under the impression that during the last session, we had voted the sum of $40,000 for such an inquiry. If I am wrong in that respect I am open for correction. When parliament prorogued I returned to my electors and told them that $40 000 had been voted for such an inquiry. Afterwards the statement appeared in the press that the Minister of Trade and Commerce was of the opinion that there were not sufficient complaints to warrant an inquiry. I do not know what grounds there were for making such a statement. At any rate, I came back to Ottawa this year with full instructions from the people of my riding to press for a royal commission to inquire into the marketing and grading of grain. I want to take up the question of grading and emphasize that point to a greater extent, perhaps, than other speakers who have preceded me. In Manitoba-the oldest province of the West and one that has been growing grain for a longer period than the other two western provinces-we have a weed element to contend with, a menace which is more formidable than Saskatchewan or Alberta have to contend with. Consequently we are doing all we can to destroy the noxious weeds. And just here let me say that the farmers in Manitoba are the best farmers in the West because they have had a very much longer experience. And we are doing everything in our power to eliminate weeds, but we have a very hard proposition on our hands and we cannot eliminate
them to the extent I would like. So, therefore, the grading affects us to a larger extent than it affects the people in Saskatchewan and Alberta. This fall, I think, we grew one of the best crops in the southern part of Manitoba, which I have the honour to represent, that was ever grown in that province, and at the same time we have received lower grades this year than in any year I know of. Even in 1916, when we had an epidemic of rust, we really received better grades than we did this year, and, of course, our grievance is much more prominent than the grievance in any other part in western Canada, for the simple reason that we are very close to the boundary.
I live only 22 miles from the boundary, and I have taken wheat to Pembina, on the American side, and my wheat would grade No. 1, at Pembina, but on the grading market in Canada, it would grade No. 3 and No. 4, so that being so close to the line does not conduce to the farmer receiving justice in regard to the grading proposition.
I received before I came to Ottawa, resolutions from practically every municipal council in the county of Provencher, and I know that copies of these resolutions have been forwarded to the Prime Minister; at least, the councils intimated to me they were sending them. The municipal councils represent all the people in the country, and I think that these resolutions are not passed lightly. Before they pass those resolutions, they study the question, and they hear plans discussed, and so forth, and I do not think they would pass these resolutions, unless they knew what they were doing.
I think the appointment by the government of a parliamentary committee was a good move, but if the parliamentary committee were going to give the grain trade a thorough investigation, we would be here until this time next year, because we cannot hold a thorough investigation in Ottawa. You must go through the country and find out from the people who know. If you brought these people to Ottawa, it would involve a great deal of expense, and there is no doubt, if that were done, the Prime Minister and his colleagues would not be able to attend the Imperial Conference next June.
The kind of commission that we in this corner of the House desire-and I think the government should give us all the support possible-is not a political commission, but a commission of men who know the grain trade and have the interest of the country at heart. In my opinion, a political commission is no good and has no right to be appointed at any time. We want a commission that will
Marketing oj Grain

bring our recommendations to the government, so that if the Grain Act needs to be amended, the recommendation of this commission, which would be a royal commission, will be put into the Grain Act, and will relieve the Canadian farmers. I might offer a suggestion. We have a commission inquiring into the lake freight rates to-day. If the government consider that commission is competent to inquire into the marketing and grading of grain, I would throw out the suggestion that, when they are through with their present work, they keep on investigating and do not stop until the people of
5	p.m. the West are getting justice in the grading, marketing and mixing
of grain.
Hon. Sir HENRY DRAYTON	(West
York): I have been waiting in the hope that the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) would make a statement to the House and save further debate.	Hon.
gentlemen know that we had this all threshed out last year, and at the request of the government, we put through a vote of $40,000, if I remember rightly. Again, if I remember, we had the whole matter discussed one evening, when many of my hon. friends to my left were present, and when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) told us, as I recollect it-hon. members will correct me if I am wrong-that in -view of the fact that the Progressives, as well as the official opposition, demanded this investigation, it would be held. Well, of course, the government have been very busy. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce has been out of the country a great deal, but he is here now -they are all home-and I was in hopes that we could be told that the investigation would go on.
Something has been said by an hon. gentleman to my left to the effect that they are glad that something is now going to be done. Well, we tried to do something and we were stopped. It was said we wanted to get a special organization-a political organization. We asked Mr. Wood-Mr. Henry Wise Wood -of Alberta, to act as chairman of that investigating commission, and he would not act. We thought that if we put him in charge of it he would at least see it was not political. He would be there and would be in charge. Failing to obtain Mr. Wood, we then asked Mr. Stewart to take charge. Mr. Stewart has been described more recently as a representative of the farmers on the railway board, but he declined. We did not want any political commission. However, that is all

old history. We thought the grievances of the West ought to be properly inquired into, and that any possible remedy that the West was entitled to ought to be given to it. We still think so, and I hope my right hon. friend, the Prime Minister, will now tell us that the vote of last year is going to be put into effect, that the government still are where they were last year, and that the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce will be given immediate effect.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
It was not my intention to take part in this debate, but it seems to me one important feature has been omitted in the remarks that have been made, and that is the effect that this investigation might have on immigration matters. We have heard a great deal said during this session on the vast number of our people that were going to other countries, especially to the United States, and what should be done to keep these people here. It seems to me that if this question which is before us this afternoon is properly settled, it will afford some solution to that problem and assist us in keeping our people on the land. I come from the Lethbridge constituency, where we are engaged in a great irrigation project. Somewhere in the neighbourhood of $8,000,000 is to be expended in that country in placing those farmers in a position where farming in the future will be a permanent success and not be subject to all the ups and downs that have been experienced there during the last twenty years.
I want to acknowledge here some real and valuable assistance we have had in our labours from the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart). We have sent men into the United States in an endeavour to get settlers to come in and take up surplus lands in the irrigation districts, and in this connection I would read a few lines from a letter which I have received from a friend who was in the United States engaged in that work. What I shall read has an important bearing on this discussion. It is dated from Oakland, and reads:
As you know I am down here to try to interest people in the Lethbridge Northern and I have had some success as far as interest is concerned but the people that would come have no money and those that have money see no real benefit in changing. I just want to call your attention to some of the things I can't explain to their satisfaction. Why fat steers at Calgary are selling for 3 to 4 cents per pound when they are worth 10 to 11 in Chicago? There is a man out north of here feeding Canadian stockers he bought at Minneapolis and says they are the best feeders he ever fed but he says where does the Canadian farmer get off that raises them? This country would take every steer for sale in Canada at a good price if it was not for the tariff. The farmers are getting $1.10 for wheat that would not make chicken feed, why do we have to take

Marketing of Grain
80 cents for No. 1 Hard when the farmer hero gets $1.10 for worse than chicken feed? Ask the Minister of Agriculture. They also ask the rate of interest and when I tell them 8 per cent they say "no Canada for
me."	,
I thoroughly appreciate and endorse the action of our government in proposing this com' mittee for this session to make a special investigation into these matters affecting agriculture. But, as has been pointed out by the mover of this resolution (Mr. Millar), it is hardly likely that that committee, within the short period available in this one session, could in any wise be able to cover the ground of the complaints raised this afternoon. I think what is needed is a royal commission to investigate this whole subject in as thorough a manner as possible. The subject is one that has been discussed up and down this chamber for the last four or five years. Not only last session was it under discussion; from the reading I have done of previous Hansards which have been sent me, I find that this same discussion has been going on for the past few years. Now, let us get down to the bottom of the whole thing and have it settled. It is the most vital question we have to deal with today, and bound up in it is the question of immigration, in fact, the question of the whole future of this country. It is a matter of patriotism that a royal commission be appointed to look thoroughly into the subject.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
I think the hon. member
for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) is to be congratulated on bringing this important national subject to the attention of the House. I do not know any hon. gentleman more capable of dealing fully and fairly with the question than the member whose name is associated with the resolution. Grain inquiries are not new events in Canada. We have had a number of them, some national, some provincial, practically all of them, I think, considerably effective, and certainly all of them of an educational character. The first one I can recall was conducted in the year 1899. It was preceded by the action of a private member, the late Senator Douglas, who inti oduced into this House a private bill dealing with the grain trade. Previous to that we had had no legislation governing the warehousing, transportation and sale of grain, except what was called the Manitoba Inspection Act. The government of that day assured the late Senator Douglas that if he would withdraw his bill they would take the matter up at a subsequent session and during the recess have an investigation into the trade, bringing down later a bill based on the recommendations of that investigation. I remember quite well the personnel of that com mission, which created a great deal of interest throughout the West. People had been harassed and were not only filled with suspicion but were absolutely certain that things were not all well and this being the first commission of its kind it can well be understood with what interest it was received. The late Judge Senkler of St. Catharines, was appointed chairman of that commission and his colleagues were three gentlemen from Manitoba, all still alive, Mr. C. C. Castle, now in British Columbia, Mr. Lothian and Mr. Sirrett. I forget who was the secretary. They conducted the usual inquiry, travellm1-about the country, and created a great deal of interest, especially among the farmers. I travelled myself some fifty miles on the prairies to give evidence, and I felt when I went home that I had not spent the time in vain. When the recommendations came down, and subsequently the legislation based thereon, I was convinced that it was perhaps one of the most successful investigations that had ever been held in connection with this important industry. Notwithstanding the very thoroughness of that inquiry, however, time seemed to reveal certain weaknesses in the act. No matter how you legislate, it is said that some people can always drive through the law. And in the year 1906 another agitation sprang up for a further inquiry. I had the honour of recommending to the government of that day that the present member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) be not only a member, but chairman, of that commission; and I have no doubt that the opportunities he had at that time of investigating the trade, not only of Canada but of the British Empire, as well as the practical knowledge we had of the producing end, have enabled him to gain that familiarity with the subject which it is evident he has to-day. In 1908, there were a number of other commissions, all more or less important. One of them was provincial, appointed by the province of Saskatchewan, and resulted in the present co-operative elevator system in that province. Later on we had the commission of 1921 which has been referred to by the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton). It is true that the operations of that commission were estopped by injunction proceedings, and it has occurred to me, since attention has been drawn to the fact, that before any more royal commissions are appointed it might be well for the status of the federal government to be established in order to ascertain how far we can go in these matters. There is no doubt that there is a federal jurisdiction; but apparently the royal commission could not go the limit of the
Marketing oj Grain

present Grain Act in this inquiry. It would be well, therefore, for any investigation to try to avoid such an impasse as occurred - in this case, because it brings discredit on investigations generally and on the Grain Act in particular. I have no doubt that before such an investigation proceeds the necessary steps will be taken to see just where our jurisdiction ends and that of the provincial authorities begins. I would gather, however, from the remarks of two hon. members that we were to avoid duplicating the personnel of that commission-I do not know exactly why, I must admit-and that the personnel of the present lake rates commission is of the right type. If that is so, we naturally feel gratified at having pleased the House, more particularly that portion of it which is intimately associated with grain growing, with the personnel of this commission.
During the last few years not only has the agitation for a further inquiry into the grain trade been continued on the part of the producers themselves after these injunction proceedings were successful, but the Organized Buyers' Association, with headquarters at Moose Jaw, have been doing a great deal of educational work throughout Saskatchewan directed to the necessity of further inquiry, especially from their standpoint as buyers. I have noticed in the press the very radical and extraordinary statements made by them which, if true, should receive very careful attention. I have no doubt that the inquiry by the special committee mentioned in the Speech from the Throne will give representatives of this association an opportunity of being heard. At all events, I hope that will be dealt with when the committee is organized.
Might I state, Mr. Speaker, that in my opinion the spirit of this resolution is being complied with by the sessional programme? It is true that the commission to inquire into lake rates touches very slightly the particular matter mentioned in the resolution, but the paragraph in the Speech from the Throne which I am about to read is so comprehensive that I think it can be taken to embrace all phases of the grain trade. The only question is whether it is possible to get at the bottom of these matters from one central point like Ottawa, or whether it is necessary to have a commission take evidence throughout the country. This is the paragraph:
The adverse conditions with which agriculture generally is confronted in many parts of Canada, despite the abundant crops of the past year, render it desirable that a special committee, with powers to make recommendations, be appointed to look into various agricultural matters such as the mixing of grain in private terminal elevators, the marketing of farm porducts,-

To look into "the marketing of farm products." That is a very broad and comprehensive term. So I think the scope of the committee is quite sufficient to cover every phase and form of grievance. The paragraph concludes:
-the development of the live stock industry, and the possibilities of further diversification in our Canadian agriculture. .
I wish to point out at this stage that the desire of the government in this direction is already shown by the commission which has already been appointed to inquire into lake rates, and by the appointment of a special committee, the personnel of which is almost complete. I have in my pocket the names of all but three of the committee, and its full personnel will be announced, I hope, in the course of another day. The committee will be set to work immediately.
I take the ground that this special committee is necessary even though the grievances were imaginary-which they all are not, of course-simply for the educational value of these investigations. Every few years there is a new body of producers growing up who know nothing about the history of the grain trade or the former investigations of that trade, and who find our grading, inspection and sample systems very mysterious processes indeed. I remember very well in 1901, when I was first associated with the Farmers' movement of that day, going to Winnipeg as the Farmers' representative to inquire into the intricacies and mysteries of the grain exchange. I went with great trepidation, feeling I was entering a den of thieves but to my surprise I found the men engaged in the grain trade were' very much like other business men. I got to know David Home, W. W. Thompson, the warehouse commissioner, and Mr. Searle, our present chief inspector. You cannot find more upright men in any business in Canada. Later on I became acquainted with some of the grain merchants whom you would find on the grain exchange acting like so many madmen. I have no doubt hon. members have all played the parlour game imitating the grain pit, and even this mild game causes quite a lot of excitement; but when millions of bushels of grain are being dealt with the excitement in the pit of the grain exchange is easily accounted for. One can expatiate on the mysteries of the grain trade to people in a country district whose minds are harassed by a hundred other things and suggestively remark what these grain dealers are doing and that their intervention between the producer and consumer might well be dispensed with. Naturally a very bad impres-

Marketing of Grain
sion can be left on the minds of your hearers. I had an opportunity of being in the grain exchange in the city of Budapest, Hungary, and unless I had had a preparatory course in Winnipeg I would have thought that the wildly gesticulating men before me should not be at large. For the sake of its educative value alone the committee referred to in the Speech from the Throne should make its inquiry as exhaustive and complete as possible.
The question of grading and sampling is a very difficult one to handle, but if we can get men of the type of Mr. Searle at the head of affairs we have made a good start in removing the suspicion that the whole business is wrong. Many men entertain the idea that the grading system could be dispensed with altogether. In my youth in Ontario when we had any wheat for sale we took it to the local mill and sold it on sample. The owner and the miller were there, they both dug their hands into the bag, and arrived at a conclusion of the value of the contents. The value was decided by weight only, but it was a matter of negotiation between them, and was in effect a sample market. That practice is all right where the wheat is for domestic use, but for export purposes the quality of your wheat must be designated by grades, and consequently a system of grading has been worked out.
