The contract grades are Nos. 1, 2 and 3 Northern which are specified by statute. What we call the commercial grades under No. 3 Northern are set from year to year by the Grain Standards Board, and of course these grades fluctuate. No wonder it is all very mysterious to the man who has not been behind the scenes, but at the same time I do not know any better system of grading.
In the United States they have practically the same system, supplemented by what is called the sample market. In a country like the United States, where a large volume of wheat is milled at home, the sample market -in Minneapolis, for instance-is a tremendous factor. But in Canada our alternative markets are not sufficiently numerous to make the sample market a dominating factor; it is the export trade that counts, consequently our chief method of grading must be by statute or by standards board rather than by sample. You will recall that before the war a great agitation arose in the West for a sample market. The multiplicity of grades, running to fifty or sixty in number, the mystery that seemed to surround the establishing of them, the taking of the samples on which they were based, and so on, led to an agitation for a sample market such as they had at Minneapolis. That demand naturally reflected itself in this House in the demand of the western representatives-in 1911 or 1912, I think it was-for provision for a sample market. I do not think it was realized at that time just what a sample market meant.
A sample market cannot be of any appreciable value to anybody, much less the producer, unless those engaged in the trade have the opportunity of mixing the grades and the various wheats. The very essence of it is the buying of wheat which has an excess of virtue over the standard grade and mixing it with lower grade wheat. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, in our determination to progress we sometimes take a mistaken step; at times we learn only by finding out that we are wrong. So that action was taken, at the request of the western members of the House, to provide for sample markets-and that always implied mixing, and now we have come back to the old difficulties of twenty-five years ago in connection with these mixing elevators.
Prior to the passing of the old Manitoba Grain Act, which is now the Canada Grain Act, mixing prevailed at Fort William to such an enormous extent that that was one of the causes which led the late Senator Douglas to bring down the bill to which I have refereed. It was felt that the mixing process was deteriorating our export wheat to such an extent that the only solution of the difficulty was to stop the business entirely. There was no way of controlling it; therefore they stopped it.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle has stated that mixing should be all right theoretically, because the owners of the mixing houses are required by law to turn out every carload up to the average grade of the public terminal elevator. That sounds pretty reasonable; in fact, it is almost more exacting, you would think, than the result would be in the case of the terminal elevators, because they have to turn out nothing less than the minimum.
Now, I find that quite competent men in the trade, mere who are probably better versed in it than any of us here, differ as to the mixing. Of course, a man who is engaged in mixing is invariably in favour of it, otherwise he would not be doing it. The man who grows the grain, especially if he is feeling hard hit at other points, is likely to suspect that there is some immense advantage accruing to the man who does the mixing, with corresponding detriment to the grower himself. Is it possible to take out, say one-third of the best of the wheat, one-third of the contents of a car showing quality over and above the straight grade -is it possible, I say, to take this out and have a residue as good as if there were no
Marketing oj Grain

mixing? Let us get it down to a simple illustration that we can all understand: if you had a dozen apples on that table and you took out the six best apples, could you possibly have as good apples remaining as you have taken out? It cannot be done. We may talk wisely about mixing elevators; we may say it is the only system by which export can be kept uniform and that no harm is done to the producer; we may say that on the other hand we are establishing an industry that is so profitable that it will bid up for these off-grade cars and that a part of the benefit will then be transferred to the producer. Well, I will guarantee that there is no hon. gentleman present who, even with the aid of the most powerful X-ray, has ever been able to see any benefit come to the producer as the result of mixing.
I know there are some men who know more about the grain trade than I do who take an exactly opposite position and say that mixing is all right. I know, too, that some of these gentlemen have the complete confidence of the Progressive group-and, indeed, of everybody who knows them. Well, if doctors disagree, who is to decide? It shows the necessity of reviewing this whole question thoroughly before coming to any hasty conclusion. There is nothing to be said . against anyone for having carried out the wishes of the West in the matter of the establishment of a sample, market. We tried it, and it is only by trying things that you get anywhere.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. minister, but what he says there is not quite correct. At the meeting in June, 1917, when the grain commission decided to put the sample regulations into force, the Canadian Council of Agriculture, representing the organized farmers of the three prairie provinces, objected to that being done.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext: I did not mention it with the idea of blaming anybody. I will put it this way: the western representatives of that day-I cannot recall who they were-[DOT] thought they were voicing the public sentiment of the West when they agitated in this House for a sample market. It is a reflection on no one; we often have to retrace our steps. There is no other way of trying some things. Take the Hudson Bay railway; there is no way of proving whether or not it is feasible except by trying it.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
May I point out to the hon. minister that when the act was amended providing for sample markets, it was not made obligatory; it was simply laid there for the use of those who desired to have it. It is

there to-day and may be used if there is a desire to use it. It was not forced upon an unwilling public.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext: I have not the act before me, and I speak subject to correction, but my hon. friend knows that certain changes were made in the act that were construed to mean that the right of mixing went with the sample market. Anyhow, everybody believes in its being practised-

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me, there is an impression going forth from his words, now, I think, in this House, that when the act was amended this parliament placed the seal of approval upon the principle of mixing. I submit to him in all fairness-and I think he will make himself clear on that point-that that is not the case. All they did was to provide, because of a widespread agitation in favour of it, for a sample market.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext: I am not aware whether it was the government prior or subsequent to 1911 that was responsible for it, but that is immaterial.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext: It was years after. The sample market was not created till about 1914 or 1915.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
Anyhow, the point is that the sample market means nothing unless it implies mixing; there is no question about that. It is a dead letter otherwise, and I think a great many people did not understand that. I am not trying to reflect on anybody; I am simply trying to give the facts. If there is any construction to be placed on my remarks, they are of an extenuating nature with regard to anybody who was responsible. I happen to have taken the other side, and I have taken it all my life. You cannot eat your cake and have it; you cannot take the good out of your wheat and have as much good remain in the residue. It has often surprised me, Mr. Speaker, that this custom of mixing has not been complained of more in the United Kingdom. I can recall the time when my hon. friend from Qu-Appelle went overseas and found, as others have found, that our wheat arrived there in a very satisfactory condition, but the whole, or I will say, three-quarters of the milling trade of eastern Canada will not order out of those mixing elevators if they can get wheat out of the ordinary terminals. Do you think they do not know when they get value? Is it possible for a miller who has been in the business for years not to know what kind of raw product makes the best flour? I am told by the secretary of the Dominion Mil-

Marketing of Grain
lers' Association himself, who is to-day in Ottawa, that the milling industries of the East avoid buying out of these mixing elevators every time they can. That may not apply this year, because there is nothing bad to mix with the good wheat, for 70 per cent or more of the wheat of the West this year is No. 1 Northern, and it is nearly all in the contract grades. Consequently, mixing has gone out of business this year, because there is nothing to mix; but almost every other year you have enough low grade stuff to mix with the virtue in the high grade stuff. I have often wondered how men who should and do know infinitely more about the grain trade than I can ever possibly hope to do without going into it, can argue on behalf of mixing from the standpoint of the producer.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext: Then is it the intention of the government this year to amend the act so as to prohibit mixing and to eliminate entirely the so-called mixing elevators?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext: That will depend, I presume, on the report of the special committee, to which every facility will be afforded to get to the bottom of this question. Those gentlemen who believe in mixing will have the opportunity to give a reason for the faith that is in them, and those holding the contrary opinion will also have an opportunity to be heard, so that we can get to the bottom of this question. Then I presume that parliament will act as it usually does, on the recommendations of the special committee.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext: If the government's mind is made up so firmly as the hon. gentleman represents, why make further inquiry?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. MILLAR FOR A COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
I am only giving my own personal view. The question was raised by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, and quite properly so, and I am simply saying that gentlemen in the trade whom I know, as well as others not in the trade, hold exactly the opposite view. Consequently, we must move with the greatest caution. We should consider the matter thoroughly and get to the bottom of it. In the multitude of counsellors surely there is wisdom; I do not think that any one man has all the wisdom on this very involved and intricate question.
Just a few words on the question of grades. This year there has been a great deal of dissatisfaction in the West regarding the grading system. I can remember that in the year 1901 there was similar dissatisfaction. Every time that we have a good crop, as in 1901 or 1922, the average man knows that it is good, but sometimes before he can get his

grain threshed, climatic conditions intervene, and while the grain is still in the stook it is so badly bleached that it grades as No. 3 Northern. We cannot see the point of it. Wheat that at the beginning of the season graded No. 1 Northern and sometimes No. 1 Hard, after one or two snowstorms, or perhaps even a rainstorm and exposure for five or six weeks in the stook, would be graded as No. 3 Northern. The miller will tell you the reason.

How do you account for wheat grading tough when there never was any rain except in June? Along the Red River valley we had most of our threshing done before the rains, but after one rainstorm in the West our grain was graded as tough.

I had a note on the tough question, and it is a tough question, but first with respect to the bleaching. I may say that the questions of bleached grain and tough grain are the two outstanding questions around which so much dissatisfaction revolves. The exterior of the grain is so wrinkled and bleached with the weather -sometimes I have seen grain actually frozen in the stook after it had been dry enough to thresh-that it looks as if it had been frozen before it was cut. No miller can extract as high a percentage of flour out of that grain as he could if it was not wrinkled. It has lost part of its commercial value, because there is no machinery for getting the maximum amount of flour out of it. But that is a miller's question. I can understand why the wheat would be graded down, although I did not at one time in my life. The wheat being mine I naturally saw it with a friendly eye, and I could not see how wheat that was perfectly good at the outset when it was cut was going to deteriorate in six weeks. I wanted the grade the wheat was at the outset.
I do not think the minister got my question right.

I am coming to that, but I am leaving the tough question till the last. I have had the opportunity, might I say, for over thirty years of being closely identified with the grading of grain, through being a member of the Western Grain Standards Board, and every year except last I was able to attend its annual meeting in Winnipeg. I think there is more real abuse in the disposition of that tough grain than in anything else I know. What are the facts?
Marketing pj Grain
I have just forgotten the percentage of moisture that is permitted in wheat-
Fourteen per cent.

I think we follow largely the practice of the United States, and
1	think they operate on the basis of 13 or 14 per cent. If there is excess moisture over that, it is graded as no-grade or as tough; it is moist, or it is tough. There are two degrees of toughness: one is slightly tough, and the other is so tough that it has to go to the dryer. There are thousands, and in some years, tens of thousands, of bushels of wheat with so little excess moisture that even though it goes no-grade, it can still be mixed with perfectly dry grain, which absorbs the moisture, and it all goes as straight grade. Every hon. member knows that. Well now, if my hon. friends were in the business, I have no doubt they would say that that was a fine way of dealing with this no-grade stuff. Here you have a dry wheat with a slight amount of moisture below the maximum, and here you have one with an excess of moisture. What is to prevent you mixing the two and producing a straight grade. At the last Standards Board meeting I was at, this question was very thoroughly discussed, and particularly in its relation to sprouted grain. What amount of sprouted grain is going to condemn a No. 1 and a No. 2 Northern and drive it into a No. 3? It is a very fine question as to how are you going to define many of these points by law; it has to be left to the fairness or honour of the chief inspector and his subordinates. We should not leave any more to them than we possibly can, but there are some points that are extremely difficult of definition in law. For example, would you say that if there was one kernel of sprouted wheat in a bushel you should throw it into No. 3 Northern? Well, that is a matter of judgment. If the wheat was uniformly good and very superior in other respects the inspector might permit that to go into No.
2	Northern. If he does not, the grain must go into No. 3, although it is otherwise good grain. It is the same with tough wheat.

I think my hon. friend said a moment ago that he had been for a
great many years a member of the standards bureau.
A member of the Western Grain Standards Board.

I think it would be very instructive and interesting to the House if the minister would explain how this board fixes

the standard from year to year. It would largely explain many of the technical points he has been discussing.
I should be very pleased to but I want to try and get through by six o'clock. I would leave that subject until the last if my hon. friend will permit me.
It is a very important question.

Tougher than the tough. We can continue the discussion after dinner. In the meantime let me just finish my story. I have a few notes here jotted down as hon. gentlemen opposite were speaking.
Getting back to the tough grain, that is the grain that has just sufficient excess moisture in it to make it go straight grade. How should we legislate with respect to that? Should we prohibit that going into the straight grade? If you did that you would inevitably reduce its value to the man who buys it. It is a big problem and I just leave the matter there. It shows that the question is one which cannot be dealt with offhand. It is very complex and very involved, and it would take the united wisdom of the whole of this committee to bring about an improvement.- However I think improvement can be made in the law.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle said that even apart from the benefits that may be expected to spring from an investigation, the question of improving the morale of our people on the farm is well worth considering. I think I am safe in saying, without laying myself open to the accusation of anything like pessimism, that the morale of the people on the land throughout the whole civilized world, and not merely this country, is low. Anything that can be done to remove either real or imaginary grievances should be done. An imaginary grievance is often nearly as bad as a real one to the man who cherishes it, and we should not be intolerant of people when we find out their grievances are imaginary. I was closely associated with the grain trade for years, and I can appreciate the difficulties that arise when you are dealing with a question so involved. I never saw anybody yet who, on his first glimpse of it, was not ready to be permeated with suspicion because he did not understand it. The more one understands the intricacies of the grain trade, the more a lot of these mysterious things of which complaint is made disappear because they are capable then of being understood.

Marketing oj Grain
I am well acquainted with Mr. Searle, Mr. Horne and Mr. W. W. Thompson, the latter an octogenarian whose honour is above reproach. These are some of the men engaged in the grain trade. I hold no brief for them, but I think some of those who make charges are in the same position to-day that I was twenty-five years ago when I thought that no good thing could come out of the grain exchange.
Now let me endeavour to comply briefly with the request of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). Just as soon as the crop is sufficiently dry to thresh action is taken. I may say that the low grade grain, as a rule, is slower in drying than good grain, with the result that it is usually the middle of October-from that to the 20th-when the inspection department, through its various agencies secures samples of the grain from every important area throughout the Canadian west. Those samples are obtained from the threshing machines through the various channels through which we have been getting them for years. As soon as they are secured the various members of the Grain Standards Board, composed of millers, dealers, and farmers, some of whom have been serving for twenty-five years, are notified by the secretary, Mr. C. N. Bell, that the annual meeting will be held in the city of Winnipeg at a given date to fix the standards for that year. When the board meets the bags are all arranged. There are fifty or sixty bags in approximate grades. Then the members of the board proceed each with a bucket or tin to go round to the different bags, each bag having a number to indicate that it was the one from which the sample was taken. They start we will say, at No. 4, that is the first commercial grade under No. 3, and the members of the board go about and build up from the samples from various districts as near as possible to the No. 4 of the previous year, and yet having entirely different characteristics. The year before it might have been a No. 4 because, we will say, of rust-thin, meager, lean stuff, but still of quite a good color. Or it might have been graded as No. 4 because of frost. That makes it a very difficult thing sometimes to get a standard sample of the same commercial value as the standard sample for the year previous. It is quite an involved business collecting standards, but that is the way it is done. We bring the wheat into the north light and spread it on the table. Three or four samples of the same grade are selected. Then they are set out in the light and compared in order to determine which comes nearest to the No. 4 sample of the year before. Next the samples are tested 20i
in the scales for weight, and finally we have a vote on the matter and that decides the grade for No. 4 for the current year. We do the same in the case of No. 5 and No. 6. Before we do No. 5 we take all the sacks from which samples were taken-a tin pailful having been taken from a number in succession-and empty them on the floor in a big pile and mix them up together. After giving them a thorough mixing we take a sample from it and compare it with what we chose before, and if they are similar-that is to say if the sample taken when the bags are emptied is similar to that taken from the respective tin pails-a vote is taken and the grade decided upon.
That briefly is the procedure. I have seen articles in the press making great sport of it. A person with a sense of humour and an active pen can ridicule anything especially something that he knows nothing about. However we have not been able to devise a better means. The only difficulty has been that as the result of rust or frost in order to get the samples graded properly you had to add a certain amount of low grade wheat. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle and the rest of the hon. members for the West will understand why and how that is done. But in order to meet that situation one year we had two series of low grades, one low grade series, Nos. 4, 5 and 6, as a result of frost and a corresponding series of low grades as a result of rust. And there you are. There are the two of them; you pay your money and take your choice. In the actual working out it was found that when they went on the markets of the world the prices of the two were practically indentical and the result was we never tried that dual system again.
I think I have covered all the ground, and I want to express my appreciation of the moderate manner in which the whole question has been discussed, and also to assure the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, that the spirit of his resolution has either been or is being complied with. When the matter comes up for inquiry before the special committee, if it is found that their facilities for research are so limited that they cannot get at the bottom of it, it will be their privilege to make a recommendation, and go as far as they can. The sample markets are still get-at-able. A great many phases of the matter are capable of thorough investigation, but if it is found it cannot be dealt with, either on account of insufficient time, or from being operated from one centre or from another, then it will be within the province of that committee to make a recommendation accordingly, and any recommendation made, either in the direction of a fuller and more favourable investiga-
30S
Marketing oj Grain

tion, or otherwise, I am sure, will receive full consideration by the government of the day. Whatever becomes of this resolution, I may say that I do not feel strongly about it, as I think that the spirit of the resolution has been complied with. I do not think harm will be done if it passes. I leave the matter with my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakeroldname: Mr. T. W. CALDWELL (Victoria and Car-leton, N.B.):
speechtext:
It is not my purpose to prolong the debate, but I would associate myself with the mover and seconder of the motion. No hon. member who has sat in this House for the last three or four years, and certainly no member who was here last year, will doubt 5 that there have been some abuses of the Grain Act and in the handling of that very 1 important commodity which contributes so ' largely to the wealth of Canada. I think the government would be well advised to inquire thoroughly into the matter. As regards the method that should be pursued, not being so well acquainted with the grain business as are my hon. friends from the West I do not, of course, feel like making any very definite suggestions. I should think, however, that if it is found that the scope of the committee which it is proposed to appoint is not adequate- and I doubt very much whether a parliamentary committee could deal fully with the subject-the government should appoint a commission to go thoroughly into all the circumstances in order that the investigation might be as complete as possible. However, as I have said, I do not intend to offer any suggestions in that direction.
I intervene in the debate especially to urge upon the government the advisability of extending the scope of the investigation to the marketing of all farm products, particularly those raised for export, instead of confining it to wheat or grain alone. We have a serious situation in eastern Canada. While we do not grow wheat for export, we grow a crop that is as important to us as wheat is to the West. And at the present time the outlook for the potato growers of eastern Canada is serious indeed as a result of some things that possibly are beyond our control, although there are some contributing factors that can be remedied by action on the part of the government. During the past summer the government established a frost-proof warehouse at the port of St. John to facilitate the export trade to Cuba.
[Mr.Motherwell.l
I might say that it became necessary for me to do a great deal of work this summer towards getting the project carried through. I am not blaming the government, but they had information that this frost-proof warehouse was not necessary at St. John, and that information came from persons who were interested in cornering the potato export trade of New Brunswick. When I came to Ottawa and explained the situation the government, I think, were fully seized with the importance of providing these facilities at St. John.
But we are faced with what is possibly a more serious difficulty. While the United States market was open to us our shipping problem was a fairly simple one; we just shipped by the carload. But since that market has been closed to us by the American emergency tariff, Cuba has been practically the only outlet for any quantity of our potatoes. I urged upon the government last spring, apart from the providing of these facilities at St. John, the importance of giving us a regular service of the Government Merchant Marine between St. John and Cuba. I would make that representation even stronger now, because my worst fears have been realized with regard to transportation from St. John to that island. In order to ship potatoes from St. John to Cuba our shippers must charter a vessel and load it with potatoes. If they cannot fill all the space with potatoes they must pay for it anyway. This puts the export business in potatoes into the hands of a few of the largest shippers of New Brunswick. The smaller shippers are practically shut out because they cannot charter and load a vessel at each trip.
There is another condition to be contended with in Cuba; and while we have no control over the actual trade in Cuba I believe that regular sailings from St. John would enable us to overcome the difficulty from this end. To-day there is a combine in Cuba that handles possibly two-thirds of the trade in potatoes on that island. I know that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb), were he in his place, could verify the statement I am about to make, that there are a number of independent wholesale potato dealers in Cuba outside the combine who have been unable to get supplies from our exporters in New Brunswick because the Cuban combine, to whom our exporters have been shipping, absolutely refuses to take delivery of any potatoes from a vessel if there are any potatoes on it for one of the independent dealers.

I do not wish to interrupt the hon. member, but I would call his attention to the fact that he is not speaking

Marketing oj Gram
to the resolution. The question before the House has reference to the conditions of grain marketing, and the hon. member is speaking on some other subject. I would ask him to bring his remarks into conformity with the resolution.

I certainly bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker. I was merely urging the government not to limit the scope of the inquiry to grain alone, and was endeavouring to show the necessity for making it comprehensive enough to embrace the subject to" which I was referring. I should like to have an assurance from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), that when the proposed committee begins its deliberations, or when the commission, if the government decide to appoint one, is constituted, I may have leave to submit this matter for consideration. I thought this an opportune time to bring to the attention of the government the fact that there are other important exports in Canada besides grain, in the handling of which there are great abuses.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. A. STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Needless to say, the department over which I, for the time being, have control, is very vitally interested in this question. Indeed, so vitally interested are we that it is the one field that is left open, under the provisions of the Immigration Act as it stands to-day, for which we may secure settlers. Owing to the occupational test and the fact that there has not been employment for intending immigrants to Canada, and the fact that those immigrants whom we are trying to induce to come to this country must be of the agricultural class, or domestic servants, any matter that affects agriculture is of vital importance to the Department of Immigration.
It is needless to say that in these days of readjustment agriculture is suffering more severely than any other industry in this country. It is desirable that this unfortunate condition of affairs should be changed, and with a view to ascertaining if some remedies at least might be applied through the agency of government, you find in the Speech from the Throne that a special committee is to be appointed as wide in scope as that requested by my hon. friend who has just sat down (Mr. Caldwell). When proposing this inquiry it was not the intention of the government that it should be confined to the one subject of grain marketing, but rather that it should cover the wider field of all agricultural activities. My hon. friend who has brought forward this resolution (Mr. Millar) has introduced a question that is not at
all new, and in my remarks to-night I shall confine myself to his resolution.
His contention is that a special committee of this House would have neither the facilities nor the power to make the inquiry necessary to enable them to recommend a solution of the problem. Two features appealed to the government in discussing this matter. There is no desire on our part to circumscribe the inquiry in the slightest degree either with respect to the marketing of grain or to any other matter that hon. members may be desirous of having investigated as being of importance to agriculture. But we have had commissions in the past dealing with this very question, and it will be remembered that the one last appointed came to a somewhat untimely end not very long ago.
There are a few difficulties of grain marketing which it is doubtful if we can remove. Ten or twelve years ago I was directly interested in marketing grain, and I found that there is one type of farmer whom it is very difficult to protect, namely, the man who takes his grain and sells it on the street or to the local elevator. I have not yet heard of any scheme that will protect him, nor do I know whether one can be devised. We who raise and market grain in western Canada know how serious a problem that is to deal with. This year during the absence of the j Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) i I had the pleasure of looking after his department and I did not let any opportunity pass : to facilitate the movement of grain. The sending of the commission to Vancouver to; investigate when a blockade seemed imminent was for the purpose of keeping that outlet1 open if at all possible. We took some chances in that connection, and one hon. member told you the other evening that the transfer of bills of lading to allow the loading of grain freely at the port of Vancouver assisted very materially in overcoming the threatened blockade. The cleaning of grain and its storage in the Calgary elevator also helped. We are anxious to maintain the flow freely to the Pacific coast, but that does not help the very large number of farmers who sell by the wagon load throughout the whole season. Indeed, when a blockade occurs, as any farmer knows, they are the men who suffer most severely, and usually they are most remote from the points at which they market their grain. Therefore any drop in price affects those who usually can least stand the loss. But frankly, I doubt if any of us would be able to secure evidence that would assist that class of farmers.
Then the inquiry resolves itself into an investigation of the inspection and the mixing

Marketing oj Grain
of grain. The man who ships his carload of grain, and is not satisfied with the return he gets can have the transaction reviewed. You may strengthen your inspectional system, and with that I do not intend to deal.
There is a great difference of opinion on the question of the sample markets, but what I had in mind when discussing this matter in government circles was that within the confines of the membership of this House, within the confines even of the Progressive membership, there are men who know every phase of the marketing conditions surrounding wheat. I do not believe that a commission will be able to secure any new evidence bearing upon those conditions. But a committee can summon before it the grain commissioners and the grain operators, and it can get the outturn of the mixing houses as well as of the larger elevators at Fort William. It rather goes to confirm what I have always had in the back of my head in connection with grain marketing or the fixing of our samples. With all due respect to my good friend, when I was handling grain actively in western Canada I always had a suspicion that the grades upon which we sold our grain were fixed too high, with consequent detriment to the farmer who had grain to sell. I may be wrong about that. However, while I had charge of the Department of Trade and Commerce I wired my colleague (Mr. Robb) to get samples off the Liverpool market, in order, as suggested by my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) that we might have them before us for comparison when discussing the matter. Those samples will be here for the inspection of members of this committee, and we will secure all evidence available from the sources where the difficulty originates, namely, in the inspection and mixing. With that evidence before us we will endeavour to improve these facilities, if they are capable of improvement, and we will do it this session even if it requires an amendment to the Grain Act. If that evidence is not sufficient-and undoubtedly hon. members of this House will be prepared to give evidence and to suggest what evidence might be brought here of an expert character-then the government stand ready and willing to go to any length to settle, if at all possible, this very vexed question.
In my opinion we were wise, on the evidence we had in hand, to appoint a commission to investigate the lake shipping combine that we think exists to the detriment of the western farmer, and we are willing to carry on an investigation that will help to solve his difficulties in connection with the growing
fMr. C. A. Stewart.!
and marketing of his grain. The question is whether it would be better to start a commission at once upon the inquiry. I have attended many sittings of these commissions, and some of the material dealt with is not of very much value; they frequently wander very far from the point when it comes to evidence that is gathered indiscriminately. But this committee can decide what evidence is vital and what concerns should be brought here. The grain board itself should be here to show the net result of a year's operations, and with this and other information we can judge whether or not we have, through this piocess, been milked to a very large extent in connection with grain marketing.
Let me say this further thing:	In the
years when I was actively interested in this matter, we were furnished with Canadian ' samples and secured standard samples for grading in Minneapolis, and invariably, not upon expert test but with the naked eye, a difference of one grade could be observed between our standard and that of the American sample. I have not examined samples in recent years, but I assume that the same condition would exist to-day. My contention is that those who fixed the standards for the Canadian grain trade fixed them too high, with resulting detriment to the producer. When we get the samples from Liverpool we shall be able to compare them with the samples upon which our grain is graded in western Canada, and in that way I think we can arrive quickly and definitely at a conclusion as to what will be necessary to assist in the settling of this rather vexed question.

Mr. Speaker I do not wish to
make any lengthy remarks on this subject, for I do not know very much about the mixing of grain, although I am the son of a farmer. But I would like to ask the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) if he would add to his resolution, after the word "grain" in the first paragraph, the words "and potatoes." I do not believe he will refuse to grant that request. The reason why I ask him to do that is this. Our American friends are coming over to New Brunswick for potato seed. It seems that we are growing the best potatoes in Canada, and our difficulty-just as it is with the grain growers-is the necessity for an improved system of marketing our potato seed. I would ask my hon. friend, therefore, to include these words in his motion.

Is the House ready for
the question?
Question.

I would remind hon.
members that when the mover of the resolution speaks, .he closes the debate. If, therefore, any hon. member wishes to address the House on the subject, he should do so now.

If I may be allowed, in
case my hon. friend does not like to make the amendment I suggest, I would propose it myself.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is necessary for me to spend very much time in closing the debate. There seems to be a unanimity of opinion in regard to the necessity for an investigation.
The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) has just said that a commission of this nature could not bring out very much new evidence. It is some years since an investigation of this kind was held, and all the time our system has been changing. 'The mixing elevator system, methods of mixing grain, the transfer of cars and many other evils have grown up since the last investigation took place, and I feel quite sure that even those in this House wTho are best posted on the subject cannot say that they know all about these matters, or that they know what allegations are true and what are not. Several charges have been made; and none of us are certain as to their accuracy. We shall make a great mistake if we base legislations on rumors or hearsay; we should have the actual facts before us.
The hon. minister stated also that he believed our present grades were too high. I must disagree with him in that respect; I do not think we suffer from that. If one raises a superior grade of grain, it is hardly just that he should not receive the better price. If his very best grain is thrown into something which is poor, naturally he must take the average of the good and the bad. The man who raises No. 2 Northern is not injured in the least if his neighbour raises grain that is one grade better and receives a little better price.
The last speaker asked that the words "and potatoes" be added to the resolution. Personally I have not a very strong objection to the addition of these words. But it may be suggested that those who are appointed to investigate the grain trade would naturally be men who are posted in that trade, and I was wondering whether they would have the necessary insight into and knowledge of the problems which my hon. friend has in mind. I was wondering whether that matter could not be brought before the special committee. If that, however, is not satisfactory
German Reparations
to my hon. friend, and if it is thought by the House that it would be best to have the two subjects investigated by the same commission, I would offer no objection to the addition of the words suggested.
I have nothing more to say, except in regard to the personnel of the commission.
I am convinced that it is very necessary to have men on this commission who are well posted on the grain trade. I am not sure that it is always wise to depend on a lawyer to act as solicitor for a commission after its appointment. I remember one experience where one of the best lawyers in Winnipeg was engaged,-a man well known throughout Canada, than whom for ability in his chosen profession I believe there is none better, yet I have seen him badly tied up when dealing face to face with the expert members of the grain exchange. He admitted to me that his knowledge did not go deep enough. He could get at the information on the surface, but when it>
came down to the difficult matters, the men who were dealing on the exchange day after day and knew all the ramifications of the business could twist and turn and get away from him. He admitted that to me more than once. I just mention that lest it might be thought that any men in whom the public had confidence, whether they had an intimate knowledge of the grain trade or not, might be trusted to do this work provided they had a competent lawyer to act as solicitor. I do not think that would be wise.
I am willing to insert the words "and potato" before the word "trade" and also before the word "marketing" in the last paragraph.
Motion as amended agreed to.

subtopic: GERMAN REPARATIONS . MOTION BY MR. WOODSWORTH FOR WITHDRAWAL OF CANADA'S CLAIMS

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Centre Winnipeg) moved:
subtopic: GERMAN REPARATIONS . MOTION BY MR. WOODSWORTH FOR WITHDRAWAL OF CANADA'S CLAIMS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is in the interest of world peace that Canada should withdraw all claims on Germany for reparations.
He said: One perhaps almost hesitates to introduce a motion of such far-reaching importance as this, on a question on which there has been comparatively little discussion in our Canadian press. However, anyone who has been following the situation at all as it has been discussed in the Old Country papers must recognize that we in Canada have a certain responsibility with regard to the Old World situation. I feel that since we were asked to participate in the great world war we ought to have some voice at this time in
German Reparations

deciding what our policy toward European affairs shall be, and especially as to our attitude toward the Peace Treaty of Versailles which concluded the war, and which in the judgment of a great many is very largely responsible for the chaotic conditions that prevail in Europe to-day.
I cannot discuss this resolution without discussing to a certain extent at least the Peace Treaty of Versailles, and also the war itself. One difficulty is that our Canadian people have had comparatively little discussion of the various aspects of affairs in Europe during and since the war. We have been perhaps inclined to say: Great- Britain is at war, or Great Britain has adopted such and such a policy, and we must follow the lead of Great Britain. I think perhaps the time has come when we ought rather to say: Since we have a certain responsibility in this matter, we must think out these questions for ourselves, and determine each on its own merits. I remember very well being in England during the time of the Boer war and hearing its merits discussed very freely in halls of various kinds, as well as reading the discussions in the newspapers. As you all know, at that time Lloyd George was among those who were bitterly opposed to the Boer war, and I think later events have shown that he was in the right. On my return to Canada, after the war was over, it was almost a shock to find that the people of this country had absolutely refused to consider any other than the one point of view. They said "England is at war, we must rush to her defence"; and apparently they were greatly perturbed if anyone suggested that there could be any other policy than that which happened to have been adopted by the party which was then in power.
Now with reference to the reasons alleged why we went to war. We were told that we went to war because Germany invaded Belgium, and it was only later that we discovered that Canada had been committed to war two or three days before Germany invaded Belgium. I think the Americans, probably, have been greatly excited during the last few months since they have learned more definitely the cargo that the Lusitania bore; not that anyone is exonerating Germany for the attack, but they are understanding a little bit more fully some of the circumstances that surround the various events of the war.
Further we ought to remember very clearly that whilst certain policies may be arrived at in Great Britain, these may in fact represent the conclusions of only a small section of the British people-possibly the conclusions only of her diplomats or her great financiers. Some

of us take the ground here that the interests of the common people of this country are not identical with the interests of the moneyed kings of this country; and a great many of the people of England, as shown by the last election, are also taking the ground that we ought not to follow the great financial leaders of Great Britain. If we criticize British policy, we are criticizing the policy not of the great masses of the people of Great Britain but the policy of a certain definite section of the people of that country.
Further I think, perhaps, it were well that when we refer to Germany we should, as far as possible, dispel from our minds the idea of the Germany which was conjured up during the war. Germany is no more a single entity than is Great Britain. Rather is it composed of a very large number of sections of people, very widely diverse in character. The Germany of the junkers and the war lords is one Germany and, I think, a Germany that very few of us here have any use for. But that is not the Germany of a large majority of the people. I remember that even during the heat of the war there was one man, at least, who stood up in the Reichstag and there suggested that war credits should not be voted, Karl Liebnecht, who was at that time hailed as being the bravest man in Europe. He represented another type of Germany, a type that was at that time protesting against the carrying on of the war.
However, I should not like to think so much of the Germany of the past, but rather to cal! attention to the fact that we have to deal since the war with a new Germany. Some among us have said that the Kaiser was responsible for the war, but we must remember that the Kaiser has been deposed, that the German people themselves have repudiated him and some of the war lords that were associated with him, and the policies which they represent. We are dealing with another Germany than the Germany that went to war. More than that-and this is the most important point it seems to me that at this stage we should keep in view-the indemnities which were saddled upon Germany by the Peace Treaty of Versailles are to be extended throughout the life time of another generation. Little German girls and boys playing around -if they play in Germany these days-are to be asked to pay reparations which simply means to give of their time and effort to pay for what men, for whom they had no responsibility whatever, were guilty of. And as we look forward to these payments extending away along through the years to come, it seems to me we may well pause and ask whether it is right, whether it is in the in-

German Reparations
terests of world peace, that we should attempt to carry out a programme of this character.
I should like to place this resolution frankly on the basis of the interests of world peace. We must rise above the old war-time viewpoint of one nation or empire set against another nation or empire, and think of the actual situation as it presents itself to-day and the extent to which we can establish a greater measure of good will and peace in the world of to-day. I take it that the Treaty of Versailles which closed the war was based on the theory of Germany's sole responsibility for the war, and I must ask your indulgence if I go into the matter a little on this point. Lloyd George said on March 3, 1921:
For the Allies, German responsibility for the war is fundamental. It is the basis upon which the structure of the treaty at Versailles has been erected, and if that acknowledgement is repudiated or abandoned, the treaty is destroyed. We wish, therefore, once and for all, to make it quite clear that German responsibility for the war must be treated by the Allies as a chose jugee.
But murder will out. You cannot always fool the people in these great concerns, and the publications which have been given to the world in recent years will, I think, indicate clearly to any unprejudiced man who studies the documents that are brought to our notice that Germany should not bear the blame forced upon her in the Peace Treaty because she is not solely responsible for the war. I am not standing here as in any sense whatever exonerating Germany for the dastardly part she played in the war-I want that to be clearly understood-but at the same time I say that we must not hold Germany solely responsible for it. Mr. A. J. Nock in 'a little book The Myth of a Guilty Nation which may be found in the Parliamentary Library has summarized the statements which have been given to the world recentfy. I may say that these statements are well documented if any of you are interested in reading them or in trying to follow them out in detail. Let me give these statements in brief:
1.	The British and French General Staffs had been in active collaboration for war with Germany ever since January, 1906.
2.	The British and French Admiralty had been in similar collaboration.
3.	The late Lord Fisher (First Sea Lord of the British Admiralty), twice in the course of these preparations, proposed an attack upon the German fleet and a landing upon the coast of Pomerania, without a declaration of war.
4.	Russia had been preparing for war ever since 1909, and the Russian and French General Staffs had come to a formal understanding that Russian mobilization should be held equivalent to a declaration of war.
5.	Russian mobilization was begun in the spring of 1914, under the guise of " tests," and these tests were carried on continuously to the outbreak of the war.
6.	In April, 1914, four months before the war, the Russian and French naval authorities initiated joint plans for maritime operations against Germany.
7.	Up to the outbreak of the war, Germany was selling grain in considerable quantities to both France and Russia.
8.	It cannot be shown that the German government ever in a single instance, throughout all its dealings with foreign governments, demanded or intimated for Germany anything more than a position of economic equality with other nations.
Mr. Lloyd George said on December 23, 1920:
The more one reads memoirs and books written in the various countries of what happened before the first of August, 1914, the more one realizes that no one at the head of affairs quite meant war at that stage.
It was something into which they glided, or rather, staggered or stumbled, perhaps through folly, and a discussion, I have no doubt, would have averted it.
Here we have a man occupying a most responsible position in the British Empire, a man who is credited with having done more than any other man in the prosecution of the war, coming out after the war is all over and saying that they simply stumbled into it, and that a discussion might have prevented it. Ex-Premier Nitti, in his book, Peaceless Europe, says-and he was another, let us remember, who was in the midst of things, and who had inside knowledge of what was transpiring at the time of the Peace Treaty, and who has intimate knowledge of the events of the war:
When our countries were engaged in the struggle, and we were at grips with a dangerous enemy, it was our duty to keep up the morale of our people and to paint our adversaries in the darkest colours, laying on their shoulders all the blame and responsibility of the war, but after the world conflict, now that Imperial Germany has fallen, it would be absurd to maintain that the responsibility of the war is solely and wholly attributable to Germany and that earlier in 1914 in Europe there had not developed a state of things fatally destined to culminate in a war.
Let me again remind you that it was in the Peace Treaty of Versailles, that we had the arrangement with regard to reparations which we deal with in our resolution. It was the very basis of that Treaty of Versailles that Germany was solely and wholly responsible for the war, a position that is abandoned by at least two of the premiers responsible for the drafting of that treaty. Now it is quite obvious that we in Canada are in a position-

speechtext:
I shall read again, if I must, the passage which I have already quoted to the House.
The more one reada memoirs and books written in the various countries of what happened before the 1st of August, 19H, the more one realizes that no one at the head of affairs quite meant war at that stage. It was something into which they glided, or rather staggered and stumbled, perhaps through folly, and a discussion, I have no doubt, would have averted it.
That is very different from his earlier statements of a great conspiracy of which Germany has been guilty. It is very different from the thought that Germany is, as Premier Nitti had said, wholly and solely responsible for the war.
In Canada, during the war, we had no opportunity, as neither had other nations, to discuss the real causes of the war; in fact, it became a crime to discuss the causes of the war. Quoting the law, I find the provision:
It shall be an offence to print, publish or publicly express an adverse or unfavourable statement, report or opinion concerning the causes of the present war, or the motives or purpose for which Canada or tho United Kingdom of Great Britain or Ireland, or any of the Allied nations entered upon, or are prosecuting the same, which may tend to arouse hostile feeling, create unrest, or unsettle, or inflame public opinion.
Now that the war is over w'e have an opportunity almost for the first time to discuss publicly the real causes of the war, and perhaps we do so even yet in a spirit of prejudice which it is extremely difficult for any of us to overcome, it is only the seriousness of the situation in Europe which forces us to enter upon a question of this kind.
As to responsibilty for war, might I call to vour attention a very excellent pamphlet, which some of you probably have, published by Mr. John S. Ewart, K.C., entitled Canada and British Wars. Few of us have had the opportunity of studying closely the many documents which have been put forward in recent years. We all recognize that Mr. Ewart is a very profound student of constitutional history and of European affairs. Mr. Ewart distinguishes between what is called the predisposing causes and the precipitating causes. Let me quote a paragraph or two with regard to the predisposing causes, the general situation which existed in Europe when the war broke out-
Aa already indicated, distinction ought to be made between the predisposing causes-I prefer to call these the roots-of the war, and the precipitating causes. The whole subject is much too large for treatment here. I must content myself with stating-very' shortly, and therefore, inadequately,-the conclusions, at which, 
after prolonged study of the immense mass of material now available, I have arrived.
1.	Tho chief of the predisposing causes in western Europe was the desire of France to repossess herself of Alsace Lorraine, which had been taken from her in a war which she had precipitated.
2.	The chief of the predisposing causes in eastern Europe was the inclusion of Bosnia and Herzegovina in tho Austro-Hungarian Empire. For the inception of that situation (Berlin Conference 1878), the United Kingdom and Austria-Hungary were principally responsible. For its development Austria-Hungary was alone responsible.
3.	The predisposing causes, as between the United Kingdom and Germany were (1) German competition in manufactures, trade, mercantile marine, and war navy; (2) the substitution of Germany for France (the British traditional enemy in western Europe) as the potential aggressor upon Belgium and Holland, and the consequent establishment of a menace upon the North Sea coasts; and (3) the substitution of Germany for Russia (the British traditional enemy in eastern Europe) as the potential aggressor upon Constantinople and India.
4.	A general predisposing cause was the erection of Europe into two vast military camps, for which all the Great Powers were, in varying degrees, responsible.
In giving the situation which prevailed immediately on the eve of the war, let me turn to Lord Loreburn, who was in a splendid position to know the situation. He says-
Serbia gave to the Austro-Hungarian Empire, cause of just offence, as our ambassador frankly admits in his published dispatches. We (England) had no concern in that quarrel, as Sir Edward Grey says in terms. But Russia, the protectress of Serbia, came forward to^ prevent her being utterly humiliated by Austria. We were not concerned in that quarrel either, as Sir Edward also says. And then Russia called upon France under their treaty to help in the fight. France was not concerned in that quarrel any more than ourselves, as Sir Edward informs us. But France was bound by a Russian treaty, of which we did not know the terms, and then France called on us for help. We were tied by the relations which our Foreign Office had created, without apparently realizing that they had created them.
Reference is here made to those secret treaties, which were not known to the world generally until they were published 9 pm. by the Bolshevik who had obtained access to the archives in Petrograd. I have never yet seen these secret treaties published in any Canadian newspaper. They were first published, I think, in England in the Manchester Guardian, a reliable old paper which we all know. They were not sent broadcast to this country, and there are those who do not yet know of the serious nature of these treaties, which had a great deal to do with tying us to France and Russia and thus preventing us from acting at the moment when possibly war might have been avoided. But we have to deal with other treaties which were made in the course of the war. I want to quote from a man whom I regard as a high authority, Mr. E. D. Morel, who, by the way, it is of interest to remark,

German Reparations
defeated Mr. Winston Churchill. And this was one of the questions which were to the fore in the recent elections in Great Britain. Mr. Morel, in Foreign Affairs, says:
In this period it has been demonstrated by the acts of the Allied governments that our people were grossly deceived in respect to the motives proclaimed by those governments in waging the war and in rejecting overtures of peace.
For all those to whom authentic information was accessible, the demonstration had been complete long before the end of the war. From the date of the secret treaties between the Allies, the war became a war for loot.
Mr. Lloyd George, speaking at the Queen's Hall, August 4, 1917, said:
What are we fighting for? To defeat the most dangerous conspiracy ever plotted against the liberty of nations; carefully, skilfully, insidiously, clandestinely plotted in every detail with ruthless, cynical determination.
To continue:
And that was very early in the day, although their existence only became known (in part) at the end of 1917, through the Manchester Guardian. It is doubtful whether the general public ever knew of them at all, i.e., in any comprehensive sense. Secret negotiations began between the Allied governments for the division of enemy territory and resources almost immediately after the war broke out. By the spring of 1915 the British government had consented to the Tsardom realising its secular ambition, i.e., the acquisition of Constantinople and the Straits, receiving in exchange a large slice of Persian territory-Persia not even being an enemy; Italy had been induced to enter the war by a treaty ensuring the break-up of Austria-Hungary, with large territorial concessions to Italy in Europe and in Asia. All through 1915 and the summer of 1916 the bargaining with Rumania continued, and was finally concluded in August of that year, which also saw the conclusion of the secret bargain with Japan at China's expense. By the spring of 1917, Russia and France had made their arrangements for the- division of Germany, which would have brought Russian Cossacks to within sight of the Oder. When Mr. Lloyd George was declaiming in the Queen's Hall, in August, 1917, about defeating a German "conspiracy" against the liberty of nations, a series of secret pacts, constituting a more flagrant invasion of the liberty of nations than Napoleon ever dreamed of, were lying in the safes of the Foreign Offices of London, Paris, Petrograd. Rome, Bukarest, and Belgrade. And the young men of Britain were being called from the factory, the office, and the plough to fight and die for the noblest of ideals! Has such a betrayal of a people's faith ever been recorded?"
Let me again say that in his treatment oi the case Mr. Morel sees that all these statements are fully documented. You can read them in pamphlets published broadcast throughout Great Britain. One other word from Mr. Morel:
In other words, it is not a case of Germany and her partner having spent far vaster sums than their potential foes before the war. Incidentally it may be remarked that although before the war the British people were supposedly the least "militarised" people in Europe, these secret commitments had made of them the most heavily taxed people in the world for war purposes. When the war came the average burden of taxation for war purposes borne by the British citizen
was much heavier than the burden of the French, German, Austrian, Russian and Italian citizen. Thus the real combination which Germany and Austria had to face was a Franco-Russian-British combination. Yet, in the decade preceding the war, their expenditure in preparedness for war fell far short even of the Franco-Russian expenditure. And, almost to the last, the German government in its blindness was convinced that Britain would remain neutral...But
the most astounding fact which French publications reveal is that, when the war broke out, the French army alone was numerically as strong as the German!

. Mr. WOODSWORTH:	If any hon. gentlemen doubt this statement they must consult the records. Mr. Francis Neilson in a book How Diplomats Make War, which can be found in the Parliamentary Library, has this to say on another point in connection wit*i the pre-war preparations:
The story of the naval conspiracy is told with extraordinary and brutal frankness by Lord Fisher in his book entitled "Memories". Lord French, Colonel Repington and Lord Haldane all confirm the story of the secret military and naval conversations between the British and French Staffs, begun in January, 1906, without the knowledge of-consent of even-the British cabinet, let alone that of the House of Commons. The reports of German diplomats recently translated and published in England exhibit the course of Allied war preparations and of the progressive isolation of Germany. The reports of the Russian Foreign Minister, Sazonof, written in 1912, show the extent to whijeh the Entente powers were even then pledged to one another and the evidence given by Marshal Joffre before the Metallurgy Committee in Paris in 1919, is conclusive with respect to the military understandings which existed among the British, French and Belgian Staffs.
Some hon. members would seem to be incredulous with regard to some of these statements. I do not wonder. Let me give an official statement concerning the question whether Great Britain was unprepared.
There is no doubt that the machinery for setting our forces in action had reached an order of completeness in detail that has no parallel in our history.
That is taken from the official documents issued by direction of the historical section of the Committee on Imperial Defence, and cp.ii be found in Naval Operations by Sir Julian Corbett. And again, Viscount Haldane says in his book Before the War:
To say, therefore, that we were quite unprepared is inaccurate.
Mr. Morel, whom I have already quoted, very well sums up the situation at the same time that he gives the source of the information, which I do not think has been very widely disseminated in Canada:
The story of British unprepared ness has vanished with the published admissions of Lord Fisher, Lord Haldane, Lord French, Sir Julian Corbett, Colonel Repington, Captain Peter Wright, and a host of others -not to mention Blunt's "Diaries". The legend of French and Russian unpreparedness was exclusively for British consumption; it was never advanced in France or Russia-indeed the feeling in French and Russian

German Reparations
official circles in the years immediately preceding the war was one of considerable confidence at the prospect of war. In any case, the legend has vanished with the publication of the Imperial Russian archives, the Belgian diplomatic dispatches, the book of the French General Buat, and that of M. Paleologue, the French Ambassador at the Russian Imperial Court, not to mention the extensive data now available concerning the Russian mobilisation and the character and composition of the Russian invasion of Prussia at the outbreak of the war. These publications and others which might be mentioned, above all the correspondence dealing with the conclusion of the Franco-Russian Alliance, have also finally exploded the myth of the "wanton attack" upon France.
I think that in view of the evidence adduced, of which I have given but a veiy brief summary, we must conclude that Germany was not solely responsible for the war.

Let me quote then, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Keynes' statement as to the conditions under which Germany laid down her arms. They were, among others:

The removal, so far as possible, of all economic barriers and the establishment of an equality of trade conditions among all the nations consenting to the peace and associating themselves for its maintenance.
(4)	Adeqnate guarantees, given and taken, that national armaments will be reduced to the lowest point consistent with domestic safety.
(5)	A free, open-minded and absolutely impartial adjustment of all colonial claims, regard being had to the interest of the population concerned.
(6)	, (7), (8) and (11). The evacuation and "restoration" of all invaded territory, especially of Belgium. To this must be added the rider of the Allies, claiming compensation for all damage done to civilians and their property by land, by sea and from the air (quoted in full above). (8). The righting of "the wrong done to France by Prussia in 1871 in the matter of Alsace-Lorraine." (13) An independent Poland, including "the territories inhabited by an indubitably Polish population" and "assured a free and secure access to the sea." (14). The League of Nations.
Before Congress on February 11, President Wilson said:
"There shall be no annexations, no contributions, no punitive damages. . .Self-determination is not a mere phrase. It is an imperative principle of action which statesmen will henceforth ignore at their peril . . .Every territorial settlement involved in this war must be made in the interest and for the benefit of the populations concerned, and not as a part of any mere adjustment or compromise of claims amongst rival states."
In New York on September 27 lie laid down the following principles:
(1)	The impartial justice meted out must involve no discrimination between those to whom we wish to be just and those to whom we do not wish to be just.
(2)	No special or separate interest of any single nation or group of nations can be made the basis of any part of the settlement which is not consistent with the common interest of all.
(3)	There can be no leagues or alliances or special covenants and understandings within the general and common family of the League of Nations.
(4)	There can be no special selfish economic combinations within the league and no employment of any form of economic boycott or exclusion, except as the power of economic penalty by exclusion from the markets of the world may be vested in the League oi Nations itself as a means of discipline and control.
(5) All international agreements and treaties of every kind must be made known in their entirety to the rest of the world.
Mr. Keynes, after showing how these different principles have been violated by the treaty, concludes:
This was the atmosphere in which the Prune Minister left for Paris, and these the entanglements he had made for himself.
This was just after the Khaki election, I
may say:
He had pledged himself and his government to make demands of a helpless enemy inconsistent with solemn engagements on our part, on the faith of which this enemy had laid down his arms. There are few episodes in history which posterity will have
less reason to condone,

a war ostensibly waged in
defence of the sanctity of international engagements ending in a definite breach of one of the most sacred
possible of such engagements on the part of the victorious champions of these ideals.
And again on this subject let me quote ex-Premier Nitti in his Peaceless Europe:
The peace treaties are the most barefaced denial of all the principles which the Entente powers declared and proclaimed during the war; not only so, but they are a fundamental negation of President Wilson's famous Fourteen Points, which were supposed to constitute a solemn pledge and covenant, not only with the enemy, but with the democracies of the whole world. . .
But it will remain forever a terrible precedent in modern history that, against all pledges, all precedents and all traditions, the representatives of Germany were never even heard; nothing was left to them but to sign a treaty at a moment when famine and exhaustion and threat of revolution made it impossible not to sign it.
Germany has already consigned all her transferable wealth; the gold in her banks, her colonies, her commercial fleet, a large and even the best part of her railway material, her submarine cables, her foreign credits, the property of her private citizens in the victorious countries, etc., everything that could be handed over, even in opposition to the rights of nations such as are known in modern civilized states, Germany has given. She has also hypothecated all her national goods...
France had but one idea, and later on did not hesitate to admit it; to dismember Germany, to destroy her unity. By creating intolerable conditions of life, taking away territory on the frontier, putting large districts under military occupation, delaying or not making any diplomatic appointments and carrying on communications solely through military commissions, a state of things was brought about which must inevitably tend to weaken the constitutional unity of the German Empire. Taking away from Germany eighty-four kilometres of territory, nearly eight million inhabitants, and all the most important mineral resources, preventing the unity of the German people, and the six million and five hundred thousand of German Austrians to which Austria was then reduced, putting the whole German country under an interminable series of controls -all this did more harm to German unity than would have been done by taking the responsibility of a forcible and immediate division to which the Germans could not have consented and which the Allies could not have claimed to impose.
What is the present situation? I have quoted ex-Premier Lloyd George; let me quote one of his latest utterances, published on January 20, last:
France has once more jumped on the prostrate form of Germany and the sabots have come down with a thud that would sicken the heart of multitudes on both sides of the Atlantic whose friendship for France stood the losses and grievances of four years' war. But what good would it bring devastated France or her over-taxed Allies? The additional coal that would be wrung out of Germany would barely cover the direct cost of collection. Although Germany bears the extra cost, the expenses of these punitive measures must all in the end diminish the means of reparations and therefore fall on the victor.

I think in the Montreal Star, and I believe I got my copy from the Ottawa Citizen. Once more permit me to quote from an article by ex-Premier Nitti, published in the European press:
In 1914 and the years immediately following, when the free and democratic peoples saw France apparently attacked by Germany, they took active sides against German imperialism. England, Italy and the United States of America stepped one after another into line and gave their blood and their economic resources to the defence of France and the rights of democracy. But later the Entente developed into nothing else than a system of violence (Gewalt-system). No German representative of the theory of might (Gewaltthrorie) has ever so glorified might as has the Entente since the end of the war. When one considers that the occupation of the Rhineland, partly by negroes, costs about four million gold marks a year and brings with it, in addition, every possible kind of evil, including the legal prostitution of German women to black men and men of other colors; that Upper Silesia, in open contradiction of the Treaty of Versailles and the mandate of the plebiscite, was dismembered; that it is to-day still considered possible by demands for senseless damages to bring Germany under an alien finance control like that endured by Turkey; that the most highly cultivated peoples of tho world have been forced under the rule of the least,-when one considers these things one can stand only in horror before this vast catastrophe that is not merely of an economic but rather one of a moral character.
In view of this situation it seems to me we ought to consider our whole policy in regard to reparations. And again, instead of voicing my own opinion, let me voice the opinion of one who knows well the conditions which obtained during the war, one of our most eminent Canadian statesmen, the Hon. N. W. Rowell.
