speechtext:
Speaking in Guelph before the Canadian and Rotary Clubs on January 26, Mr. Rowell said-I quote one paragraph:
Canada's substantial claim to a share in tho reparations is based on the inclusion of pension and separation allowances in the Treaty of Versailles. Canada should relinquish all claims under those heads, as they are not covered by the agreement under which Germany laid down her arms, and should not be included in the treaty. Further, as it is now admitted that Germany cannot pay even sufficient to cover the cost of restoring the devastated areas, any payments which might be made to Canada in respect of pensions and separation allowances would necessarily come out of the amount which should properly go to France and Belgium. If, after these deductions, there remains any further sum payable to Canada, we should be prepared to follow the lead of Great Britain and forego this amount in the interests of a general settlement of the whole
| M i. \Voodsworth.]
question of reparations and inter-Allied debts. Fortunately for us, the government of Canada, both during and since the war, has based our finances on the assumption that we would have to pay our own costs of the war, and the failure to receive any sum from Germany on account of reparations, will not involve any change in our financial program.
Now, on this question of our share in the reparations, let me point out that according to the original agreement, as Mr. Rowell has shown, the inclusion of pensions and separation allowances was not involved in the conditions under which Germany laid down her arms. There are one or two misapprehensions that should at this stage be removed. There are some who imagine that private claims for damages will be paid in Canada. I am told by those associated with the Reparations Commission that there is no intention whatever, nor was there ever any, that private claims should be paid. It is true that an advertisement was sent out asking that people in Canada who had suffered damages should send in their claims, but this was done in order that Canada might be able to estimate the amount of damages she should claim. It was not the intention that the money so procured from Germany would be turned over to private individuals. That policy was very clearly stated in the British House of Commons by Mr. Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer. In reply to a question on May 4, 1920, Mr. Chamberlain said:
His Majesty's government has given careful consideration to the position of individuals in respect of whose losses reparation will be claimed by His Majesty's government. It must be understood that tho claims to be made are claims by the British .government in respect of a wrong done to the state, and not claims by individuals in respect of private wrongs, and that the government do not act as the agents of any individual to put forward his personal claim. Any payments that may be received from Germany are therefore the property of the nation, and no individual will have any claim in law for any sum which the British government may receive from Germany in respect of reparation.
On one other point, too, I think there should be a statement made, and that is with regard' to the closely related question of the property or estates of German nationals in this country which have been seized by the Canadian government and are now being held. I believe there is a trust of something like $40,000,000 which is being administered. On this point may I quote a few sentences from the annual report of the Canadian Bank of Commerce. The president of the bank says:
In all references to it authorities on international law make it clear that our right to retain enemy property which falls within our control exists only so long: as the enemy country- fails to honour similar obligations or to restore our property.

German Reparations
Further:
It is with reference to these exceptions that difficulties are being encountered, out of which there may arise the very unfortunate conclusion that in the treaty departure has been made from principles which have been respected for centuries.
And still further:
We must not in this matter be influenced by anything but the facts, and by that honour among nations which has been displayed for centuries. It is true that the property and business interests of the Allies were sometimes very wrongfully dealt with in Germany, at least in the early years of the war, but it is also true that Germans ready and willing to settle debts directly with British creditors have been unable to do so because of the terms of the treaty. Every merchant seeking to do business in foreign countries, and every banker considerate of the credit of his country, should remember that international trade and finance are built on good faith ,and that we must avoid the possibility of these unfortunate exceptions in the treaty causing injustice and thus involving Canada in discredit.
Another point made by Mr. Rowell to which I would call attention is that if we were ever able to collect from Germany for our pensions or separation allowances, such sums would really come out of the amounts that ought to go to the building up of the devastated districts of France and Belgium. I have not been saying anything to-night with a view to arousing any feeling against France. I think, on the contrary, we may well say that if we relinquish the amounts which we claim, they might possibly go to the help of Germany in paying the amounts which ought to be paid to France and hence those districts which have suffered the most severely would be built up.
Let me very briefly summarize a few points which I should like to leave with this House.
First of all, that our claims under the Treaty of Versailles are contrary to international law as international law was understood before the war. I was reading only the other day the international conventions with regard to the laws and customs of war by land as signed at The Hague in 1899. It would seem as if we in our peace treaty at Versailles had contradicted almost all these conventions which had been drawn up, and which at that time were supposed to prevail amongst civilized nations when they were unfortunately drawn into war.
Next I would appeal on economic grounds. Canada's prosperity as that of other nations is dependent upon the prosperity of Europe. We cannot have prosperous conditions in Europe until the peace treaties are definitely modified. On that point let me quote from [DOT] one who, I think, will be considered an authority, Professor R. A. Seligman, Professor of Economics at Columbia University. In the New York Times of November 5, 1922, Mr. Seligman says:
What is the situation in the continental countries of Europe? They have no gold to remit. They cannot send us their land, railroads or factories. They have no more securities of foreign countries to turn over, as England did during the war. There is no likelihood of any substantial increase in the invisible items which they could transfer to us. On the contrary, in the present perilous economic situation there is slight probability of their receiving additional sums on foreign investments or profits on a larger merchant marine, or gains through developing banks or insurance companies; and the sums yielded by a possible increase in American travellers abroad or in the sums remitted by immigrants to this country would be only a drop in the bucket.
Again:
The truth is our debtors are bankrupt. They cannot pay now, and will not be able to pay in any assignable time. I have found no prominent business man or banker here or abroad who believes that there is any possibility of paying the debts. You cannot extract water from a stone.
But even if the Allies could pay, the final question arises: Should we demand that they pay now and forthwith? If they have the ability to pay, have w& the capacity to receive?
Still again.:
No explanation can obscure the fact that, despite the three-cornered trade, a nation's commerce must be envisaged as a totality. If the rest of the world pays a debt by exporting more goods, whether to us or to another country, it makes it harder for us to export the usual quantity of goods in return. The reason why, under normal conditions, exports are mutually profitable, is that the exporting country is thereby enabled to secure imports, that is, to buy commodities. It is a matter of give and take. But when, in order to pay an immense debt, the rest of the world has to increase its exports to us, there is nothing to call for imports in return; and with this cessation of our exports to foreign countries our factories will close, our industries will languish and a period of business depression will set in.
That is, we must realize that the world today is a unity, and that just as in the human physical system you cannot have one diseased part without its affecting the whole body, so in the world to-day we cannot injure one member without all the members suffering with it.
I do not know whether it is at all possible that I appeal on the higher moral grounds, that we take this stand in the effort to bring about better conditions in Europe. We may demand our pound of flesh, but all through the history of the world there has been another strain of teaching running that mercy is greater even than justice. We are nominally a Christian country. I wonder if we can ever learn to begin to put in practice those words which I heard no later than this afternoon from the lips of the Speaker: "Forgive us our trespasses as we forgive." I suppose it is bad form to say that. I do not often come into prayers, but I do not see why we should not begin to try to practise some of these phrases that are so often upon our lips.	It is quite true that the
amount involved, so far as Canada is con-
German Reparations

cerned, is not large. It may be true, as a good many have pointed out, that we will receive nothing anyway, but at least such an action of this kind on the part of Canada would be a certain gesture which might have some influence in other parts of the world. We read of an historic occasion on which a shot rang round the world. It is quite possible that action on the part of even a comparatively small nation such as Canada might have far reaching effects, and that our action may be followed by a somewhat similar action in other parts of Europe. Only the other day we were formally accepting the gift of a piece of land from France on which a monument might be erected to our men who fell at the front. I think none of us would withhold tribute to men who, from heroic motives, offered their all for what they believed to be the very highest and best, and yet one cannot but remember that the whole of Europe is strewn with monuments. I well recall some years ago spending a day on the battlefield of Waterloo and there seeing the great monument erected to the victors, Great Britain and Prussia, and in another part of the field a small monument, a most pathetic one I thought, an eagle with a broken pinion erected to the vanquished, France. Now the scene is changed. France is our ally for the time. Prussia has been our most deadly enemy. Before the monument is erected in France it may -well be that relations between England and France may be most severely strained. I wonder whether, after all, we can best honour the memory of those who fell on the fields of France and Belgium by erecting monuments over there, or rather may we not do more by seeking to arrange our economic and social conditions in such a way that future wars will not be brought about.
You remember how Lawrence Housman seeks to give expression to the feeing of the men who fought at the front:
We fought at Armageddon for the brotherhood of
man;
And safe within their fences the tricksters plied their trade.
'Twas the old fight we fought; and it ends as it began:
The gamblers hold their hands till the last trump was played...
And the freedom that we fought for is an unremembered tune.
Mr. Speaker, it seems, as we read history, as if the human race has climbed, by very small degrees, up the blood stained trail that has led to even the measure of civilization that we possess at the present time. Some recent developments have given to mankind a wonderful power, have given us control of machinery which might be used in the

interests of mankind or, if used by one group in opposition to the other, may spell the very doom of our race. It seems to me that on an occasion of this kind we should try, at least, to rise above the passions and prejudices of the war, the passions and prejudices that have kept the peoples of Europe apart throughout these years, and that we at this distance, somewhat removed from the horrors and chaos of Europe to-day should, in a little more dispassionate way, resolve that as for us we could, we would, do our utmost to start, things on a somewhat different path in the future. I would plead that the least we can do is to make what I have called a peace gesture and withdraw our claims to reparation from Germany.

speechtext:
I can imagine no other condition or time under which it could be as conclusively proven that "time is a great healer." Hon. members in this House, imagine, if you can, four years ago to-night, sitting deliberately and listening to a statement from an hon. gentleman such as we have heard for the past hour and a half. I want to say only a few words in regard to this particular matter, and not of necessity dealing at all with the particular question of reparations, or the question of the sums owing to Canada by Germany. I care not personally whether the reparations ever come or not, but I do be-live that there are some things that surely the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) has either overlooked or else never experienced. He spoke? of the great trouble, tribulation and hardship that would come to future generations of German children should there be insistence on the payment of these reparations. I imagine that I learned in my younger days and since from the same Book of Holy Writ as my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg, and in that I found conveyed the suggestion of an eye for an eye and that justice is eternal. Four years ago that would have been conclusively proven to my hon. friend and other members of this House, I imagine, had anyone even thought of such a thing as raising the question that we have heard raised tonight.
I wonder if my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg knows anything of the wounds in the hearts of tens of thousands of Canadian mothers that are being opened up afresh tonight, and that would, if his view carried, figuratively speaking, bleed with the injustice of the proposals that have been discussed before. us. I think it can be very readily conceded that sentiment very largely rules the world, and, looking at it from every viewpoint of sentiment, I cannot but express the view that my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg has acted in entire disregard of the feelings of tens of thousands of Canadian mothers, yea, and of Canadian fathers, in making any such proposal or indulging in any such discussion as we have just listened to. My hon. friend surely overlooked the fact that mankind in all the ages, from the garden of Eden, has, we are told, been paying the penalty for sin, for injustice, for violation of the law, and does he appeal to us as human beings, thousands of Canadian citizens, with hearts still bleeding, and expect us to forget all of our conception of human justice and right, and do the work of forgiving, whitewashing, waving these things to one side, as is suggested in his resolution? The hon. member undertook, as I understood, to show that maybe Germany was not responsible for the war to the extent that was alleged, but I would submit to my hon. friend that were it possible for this resolution to pass, tens of thousands of Canadian mothers and fathers would hear the tramp of a nation run mad with the lust and desire for conquest, marching through Belgium, and that would be the only thing that they could see was the cause of the war.
I desire to say, Mr. Speaker, that so far as I am personally concerned, I think the proposal of my hon. friend to-night is in entire disregard of the sufferings, the sacrifices and the feelings, present and future, of tens of thousands of Canadian citizens, and might I, in all seriousness, suggest that if my hon. friend is so sincerely desirous of bringing about peace and of obtaining harmony and co-operation, he will find wide scope in tb*

industrial field here in Canada, where there is ample opportunity for the exercise of his undoubted ability and great earnestness in this direction. speechtext:
I will answer my hon. friend by quoting his next statement. He pleaded on behalf of the little boys and girls of Germany. Well, what red-blooded man living to-day would not respond to a plea of that kind, whether the children were of Germany or anywhere else? But methinks there was a time when strong red-blooded men turned a deaf ear to the plea for children, boys and girls and babes. What about the advance of the German troops through Belgium and northern France? Outside of warfare waged by absolutely barbarous people, there has never been an instance in history in which there was such an utter disregard for the helplessness of childhood and the weakness of old age as characterised the advance of the German soldiery through Europe at that 21i
time. And yet my hon. friend comes to this House and says. "Let us think of the boys and girls of Germany". Why, certainly, I am prepared to meet him on that ground and discuss the resolution from that standpoint. But I think we ought also to think of the boys and girls of Great Britain, of France, of Canada, and other countries. Next, my hon. friend brought forward one of the stock arguments-well, it is not really an argument, rather let me say, one of his stock sneers at modern society, one of those soap-box references that we hear so often on the street corners, where men who have been toiling, or who perhaps are out of luck, or are misfits in society, are teased and agitated and aggravated into resentment. He trotted out the gibes about the great financial lords, and captains of industry. He based no argument on it, but he just introduced it in his speech -it will read well among certain groups of his followers and friends. They will say: Our great leader in the House of Commons has brought before the attention of his fellow members the iniquities of the financial lords of Europe.
Let me remind my hon. friend that his insinuation is baseless, for this reason. It was argued throughout the world that no great war could come. Why? Because the great moneyed interests of the world would not permit it. But I submit that in spite of the most bitter objections and in spite of all the efforts put forth by the great so-called "controlling influences" of industry and finance, this war bioke out. I am not going to rehash the discussion of why the war broke out, but I answer his argument with that statement, which no one can, I think, gainsay.
Then he quoted as the greatest authority of all, and the most outstanding-whom? Mr. Morel. What is Mr. Morel's claim to notoriety? Simply that he defeated Winston Churchill. That is the sole reason why we should accept what Mr. Morel says. As my hon. friend put it very modestly: "My opinion is no good; I give you Mr. Morel's." Now, in the long quotation my hon. friend read Mr. Morel referred to the conferences between the British, French and Belgian military staffs. Will my hon. friend deny that he called those conferences a conspiracy? Hansard will show that he did. What does he term a conspiracy? That which was published in the White papers of every one of the allied nations; everything to which he referred to-night and suggested to this House as a secret revealed because the spotless Bolsheviks of Russia had secured the archives in Petrograd. That was my hon. friend's argument. "This conspiracy was revealed." Those were his words. Revealed!
German Reparations

My hon. friend ought to know that this so-called conspiracy was revealed in 1914 at the commencement of the war and again in 1915 showing the conferences that had been held between these staffs on questions of preparation.
Then as an offset to our charge that Germany had been preparing for this war for years what did he bring forward? Britain's preparedness! And he quotes the speech of one of Britain's statesmen in that regard. Everybody knew

and well for my hon. friend, for every hon. gentleman in this House, for the whole North American continent, and for other parts of the world was it-that the British navy was prepared. Winston Churchill - whom he so slightingly refers to, and whom Mr. Morel, one of his British communistic leaders, defeated in the last general election in Great Britain-Winston Churchill abov all other men was responsible for the preparedness of the British navy. Was there any secret about it? I recall perfectly well in March 1914 one of the most lengthy and exhaustive debates ever held on a British budget had to do with the navy vote in that year, and again in 1913. And yet my hon. fiiend says there was a secret conspiracy among these nations, and that Britain's preparedness was in the nature of a crime equal to the military aggressiveness of Germany. These are the arguments, Mr. Speaker, that make one resent the presentation of a purely business proposition.
Then my hon. friend, in reply to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner), who asked him very politely and in perfect parliamentary order, would he be kind enough to give the House his own views, shielded himself behind the rather clever practice of reading the views of others. From one end of his speech to the other my hon. friend never told us where he stood on this question. But I know this much. If he goes to the city of Vancouver where he spent a few years, if he goes to the city of Winnipeg where he also spent an active period-in these cities, if he can do it with an audience just suited to him, he will tell them in most violent language where he stands on this question. I know my hon. friend's position. In this House he has conducted himself with commendable reserve. I have watched him during last session and this, and I must say I admire him. Bnt, Mr. Speaker, the language in which my hon. friend would express himself on these problems under other circumstances would be of an altogether different character. And so he was afraid to tell this House frankly where he stood on this

question. I challenge him, and I challenge everyone who belongs to that peculiar group of economic freaks, who owe allegiance to the Third Internationale in preference to the British Crown, to come out frankly and, through him, debate this question in the proper form-on the floor of the parliament of this country. If they have an opinion, this is the place to express it. I do not question a member's right to read other people's opinions on a subject while refusing to declare his own view. That is his privilege. But I do question a man's moral courage who will do it and then, under other circumstances peculiarly suited to himself, give vent to expressions of policies inimical to the welfare of this realm.
My hon. friend also addressed himself to quotations from Mr. Keynes' famous books on The Economic Consequences of the Peace and A Review of the Peace Treaty. I pay a tribute, Mr. Speaker, to Mr. Keynes, whom I look upon as one of the most thoroughly versed political economists in Europe and, perhaps, in the world to-day, a man of exceptional ability and one who has given expression to his own views in a very frank and courageous manner. My hon. friend selects a passage here and there and dovetails them into his speech this evening. Mr. Keynes once applied his arguments either in his book on The Economic Consequences of the Peace or in his famous articles in the Manchester Guardian Supplement during the past year in the manner that my hon. friend has applied them to-night. Mr. Keynes does argue-and I want to say here very frankly that in a large measure I agree with him

that the French particularly are interpreting the Versailles Treaty in a somewhat harsh and exacting manner. That is Mr. Keynes' argument in a nutshell. He labours very industriously and very effectively to prove his position.
But my hon. friend paid most of his respects to Great Britain in his insinuations. Well, Great Britain is the one country that has stood out firmly against an extreme interpretation of the Versailles Treaty by the French. Why was not my hon. friend generous enough to say that the country which has offered him protection during the whole of his life has been honourable in this regard? Why h'as he not been generous enough to say that Great Britain has been more than generous with the Germans in regard to reparations?
Then my hon. friend quoted ex-Premier Nitti of Italy. It might be well for this House to pause for a moment and ask what became of Mr. Nitti. Has he the support

of the Italian people to-day? He certainly has not. He has been completely rejected by his people.

speechtext: What about Mr. Lloyd George?

speechtext:
I was coming to Mr. Lloyd George, if my hon. friend will wait a moment. Mr. Nitti has been rejected by his people. My hon. friend quotes Mr. Nitti to bolster up his argument, and he states in a general way that the people, not the few, should rule. But have not the people of Italy recently put Mr. Nitti out of business? I will give you, Mr. Speaker, what I am quite convinced, from several addresses I have heard him make, the hon. member means by "the people." In his estimation, the people are composed of that group in each country which corresponds to the
500,000	Bolsheviks in Russia out of the 180,000,000 inhabitants of that country. In his estimation, an organized group with his peculiar economic and philosophic ideas, no matter how small it may be numerically, constitute the people of a country. We happen to believe in majority rule. While there are injustices under our present system, and lots of them, we believe that through it we get the best expression of opinion on the part of the people that up to the present it has been possible to get anywhere. No man who has followed with any degree of interest the history of his friends in Russia will be able to argue, no matter how finely spun those arguments may be, no matter how subtle and insinuating the language in which they are expressed may be, that there is anything approaching real liberty under the rule of the Third Internationale, in Russia.
Now, my hon. friend quotes Mr. Nitti. Then he says that Mr. Lloyd George used the phrase-and we all know that Mr. Lloyd George is perhaps the most apt phraser that we have on two legs to-day-that Germany was prostrate. My hon. friend seizes upon this little phrase and produces it before the House as an argument in support of his extreme resolution, yet he condemns the part played by Britain under the leadership of Lloyd George all through the period of war. I would also remind him that the very gentleman whom he produces here as an authority has been rejected by Great Britain, and particularly, Mr. Speaker, by Mr. Morel and a few other of his friends.
My hon. friend introduced another suggestion which was unworthy of him-and that is going some. He introduced that old shibboleth about the French-coloured troops on the Rhine. He is not in a position to give accurate
information on that, nor am I. But this we do know, that a great deal of the agitation regarding the supposed occupation of the Rhine by coloured troops of France is mythical and false-is propaganda by the Germans themselves. There are more official reports excusing or justifying the French government than there are condemning them. I am not going to say for one moment that French troops occupying a territory like that have been blameless; it would be utterly impossible to pick out a group of men thus situated who would be free from any action that could be questioned. But to suggest, as my hon. friend has, that France has perpetrated a crime upon civilization in her occupation of the Rhineland, is, Sir, to present an argument that has no foundation in fact.
Then my hon. friend proceeded to quote a speech of Hon. Mr. Rowell. Quoting Mr. Rowell, he said: that Canada should follow Great Britain in the matter of a policy on reparations. In his opening remarks he jeered at and condemned Canada for following Great Britain in connection with the action taken at the outbreak of war; now he comes along and supports the statement of' Mr. Rowell that we should follow Great Britain in the matter of reparations. The question whether a thing suits my hon. friend depends on whether the action taken suits his own particular mental distortion. If it fits into that peculiar state of mind into which he has forced himself in recent years, then it is all right; if it clashes with that state of mind, then it is all wrong and there is no justice, equity, reason, logic or anything else in it. " What is right is what suits my peculiar state of mind"-that was my hon. friend's process of reasoning in his speech to-day, as it is in all his presentations throughout the country- and they are many-with regard to economic problems.
Then my hon. friend makes a general sweeping charge of violation of the treaty by France. I admit very frankly, Sir, that there is ample room for differences of opinion in interpreting the Treaty of Versailles. The greatest minds of Europe and America have been struggling with that treaty for the last three years. But should we not pause before making rash and hasty assertions condemning a whole nation for its action? Should we not pause and consider the peculiar and intricate conditions under which this treaty was entered into? Here we have a world literally prostrate as the result of the war-all participants in a state of chaos. State after state complete^ disrupted; new governments and new constitutions created overnight. Under conditions
German Reparations

of that kind, a score or more of nations meet together to draft a treaty of peace; is it any wonder that this piece of machinery produced under circumstances of that kind should in after years, in times of comparative peace and coolness, be found to be more or less faulty? So it is with the Treaty of Versailles. There are very few, if an}:, who do not frankly admit that the Treaty of Versailles must in some respects' be changed and modified. But that does not warrant my hon. friend's coming before this House with a libellous charge against the statesmen who made the treaty. I believe that with few exceptions, if any, the statesmen who engaged in the titanic task of trying to weave peace and order out of chaos did their duty faithfully and earnestly and with a common desire for peace. That they have not brought peace is something for which they cannot be blamed. It certainly will not contribute to peace to have such unfounded statements flung to the four winds as my hon. friend has made here to-night, and, unfortunately, is making on all possible occasions.
My hon. friend said also that this treaty and its enforcement violated international [DOT] law. , He did not tell us in what way it did so, but he said it violated international law as it was understood prior to 1914. I am not going to question the accuracy of his statement, but I would like to know, Mr. Speaker, what respect there was for international law on the part of Germany and her allies? Was there any respect for it? Did not Germany openly declare and avow officially through her Chancellor, Bethmann-Hollweg, that Germany would ignore international law; that it was in the interests of military tactics that Germany invaded Belgium?
Now I do not say that that justifies us in violating international law, but I would draw the attention of the House to the vast difference between the violation by Germany, and the supposed or alleged violation by France and her allies. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), suggests, how could a treaty violate international law? As a matter of fact, the whole question narrows down to this: Is the interpretation of the treaty by the Allies a fair and reasonable interpretation? Then the second question is this, and it is really the most important problem that this parliament and similar parliaments have to deal with: Assuming that we interpret the treaty correctly, and fix a given amount for Germany to pay, is that amount a reasonable amount under the conditions now existing, that is, can Germany possibly pay?
I would say this to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. After a great deal of

thought upon this subject so far as my individual capacity would permit, I am prepared to advocate and support this in the House of Commons: That we should seek to determine as far as we can, and in a generous spirit, the extent to which the reparation amounts due under the Versailles Treaty ought to be reduced to meet Germany's capacity to pay. That is a fair question, and one which may properly engage the attention of every fair-minded and intelligent and unprejudiced person.
My hon. friend then says he appeals on economic grounds. His economic grounds were not stated. He did not disclose cither his own opinion, or the economic grounds upon which he wished to support his motion. The only hint of an approach to economic grounds that he gave was a general, sweeping statement that Germany could not pay, that Germany was bankrupt. I would remind him and this House that up to perhaps six months ago Germany was the most prosperous country since the war of any in the world. It is true that about six months ago, or perhaps a little longer, this prosperity broke. The inflation of her currency and the devaluation of her monetary system has resulted in more or less of chaos in Germany to-day, but it is strange that only a day or two ago the German Reichstag asked the chief bank of Germany to release-what? 'A very huge sum of gold marks that they still held in their vaults, for the purpose of stabilizing the currency of Germany, and the bank refused to release that money. My hon. friend in his statement a moment ago said that Germany had no money, or words to that effect -that Germany was bankrupt, that she had no amounts of money, that all her gold and all her resources were gone. I would remind this House that in no single instance has the industrial machinery of Germany been tampered with except by my hon. friend's German friends, through sabotage and strikes, and in no other way. Germany's whole industrial machinery is intact, whereas France, as tve know, was prostrated and devastated over very large areas, a great portion of which will never be restored, indeed cannot be restored. Mines have been wholly destroyed so that they can never be worked again. It is so with other parts of Europe other than German territory; but German machinery remained intact and is intact to-day. Does not the wealth of a nation very largely consist of the things out of which they produce, such as the land and the machinery, whether it be industrial or agricultural? Germany was never touched in one of these things.

German Reparations
Her farms, her mines, her machinery, are all intact. Her people were undisturbed except those who were fighting in the war. Compare that, Mr. Speaker, with Belgium and France and certain portions of Italy, with Serbia, with Roumania particularly, with Bulgaria and Poland. Compare the condir tions in these countries with conditions in Germany, and you have a complete reversal.
Now let us turn for a moment to the situation as far as Canada is concerned. We are faced in Canada with a huge debt, and for the size of our population and our development that debt is an appalling burden. Some day in the near future I intend to discuss it at some length, but suffice it for tonight for me simply to remind the House that that debt rests with extreme weight and with grave possibilities upon the shoulders of the people. I am not prepared to say that we should forego the claims that we have against Germany; not at all, Mr. Speaker, but I again repeat that in so far as it can be shown, supported by intelligent and accurate information, that the reparation claims from Germany are beyond her economic possibility of payment, to that extent I am prepared to consider the reduction of our claims against her. But to come forward with a resolution such as my hon. friend has moved-1 was going to say 'falsely' clothed, but perhaps that would not be parliamentary-inaccurately clothed in the argument that it is in the interests of world peace to present this resolution under present conditions, and to support his motion by such a speech as he has delivered, which was far more significant in what it left out and in what he insinuated, than in what he actually did say-such an appeal, I say, should not win any support from this. House.

subtopic: GERMAN REPARATIONS . MOTION BY MR. WOODSWORTH FOR WITHDRAWAL OF CANADA'S CLAIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the mover of this resolution (Mr. Woodsworth), and also the last speaker (Mr. Stevens). They have both presented extreme views. I hope that those who will take part in this debate from now on will endeavour to keep to the middle road.	.	.
This discussion is one of the greatest importance, I believe, to this country. I do not think that anyone will disagree with me-I know that the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) will not-when I say that the whole future of western Canada is wrapped up not only in economic peace but every possible kind of peace in Europe. If, therefore, by the cancellation of Germany's debt to us we can help to bring about that
peace, or progress just one step towards it, we shall have done a great deal.
The Treaty of Versailles which has been referred to so frequently to-night has not, I think, been glanced over at all. Let us look at it for a moment. In that treaty Germany specifically accepted responsibility for all the damage which she and the countries associated with her had done to Great Britain and her allies. On the other side, Great Britain and her allies specifically acknowledged in the treaty that the resources of Germany were not adequate to make complete reparation for all such loss and damage. The treaty did not attempt to fix the amount of damage for which Germany was to make payment, but it did provide for an initial payment on May 1, 1921 of twenty billion gold marks. This payment was to be in gold, in commodities, in ships, or, otherwise as the Reparations Commission might decide. In addition to that the remainder of the reparations to be made by Germany were to be decided upon by the Reparations Commission and were to be announced to Germany on or before May 1, 1921. On January 23, of that year the Reparations Commission reported that prior to December 31, 1920, Germany had delivered in payment of the 20 billions of gold marks referred to a large number of ships, a great quantity of commodities-I have the list with me but I do not. think I need weary the House by giving the details-and in addition all her submarine cables. The estimated value of these commodities varies very much but one thing can be said, and that is that the value fell very far below the 20 billion marks. On May 10, 1921, Germany under pressure, accepted an estimate by the Reparations Commission of the additional reparations payable which we fixed at 132 billions of gold marks, roughly about 33 billion dollars. These were to be covered by bonds in three series-A. amounting to 12 billions; B, amounting t.o 38 billions. Both of these, bearing 5 per cent interest, were delivered to the Allied governments. Series C, of 82 billions was non-interest bearing and was to have been delivered, by November 1,	1921. In addition, the
Reparations Commission decided that annual payments were to be as follows: 2 billions of gold marks and a variable amount up to 26 per cent of the total value of German exports. These payments were only sufficient to pay the interest on the bonds of Series A and B, and 1 per cent for amortization purposes, but they made no provision whatever for meeting the bonds of series C.
Now Germany made the first payment of 1 billion on time, but she at once commenced to
German Reparations

assert her inability to make any further payments. Then commenced those conferences. Conference followed conference, failure followed failure, leading up to the situation that we are now faced with. No one with a heart, no one with the realization of France's suffering, of the destruction which she has experienced, of her loss in every sense, can resent her stepping across into the Ruhr. No one who looks at the matter purely from the sentimental aspect, or from the aspect of cold justice, will blame her for her action. We all have deep sympathy for France, but in so acting did she take a wise step? None of the premiers of the other countries think it was a wise step. Only in this morning's paper I notice that an amendment to the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne is to be moved in the British House of Commons. I am not quite certain who is to move it, but the amendment, which is being prepared by Mr. Lloyd George and Mr. Asquith, advocates the appointment of a commission in which the United States would be invited to participate for the purpose of investigating Germany's capacity for reparation payments and the best methods of securing a quick settlement.
The last speaker referred to the inflated condition of the currency in Germany but did not dwell on the effect that that had on the possibility of Germany meeting her debts. May I quote in this regard the Prime Minister of England. The charge has been levelled, mostly I believe by France against Germany, that she deliberately inflated her currency for the purpose of avoiding the payment of her debt, but the British Premier speaking about this says:
Honestly I cannot myself take that view gnd for this reason: It is perfectly true that by that method of passive resistance Germany can avoid her ever paying any indemnity, but it only means what is very like suicide for Germany. I can hardly believe that any sane government would deliberately adopt that course.
Yet that course was adopted and continued until it led to some extraordinary conditions. The position of Austria in this regard is a slight degree worse, but not very much worse, at the present moment. I read some little time ago of a mortgage that had been taken out in the year 1917 in Austria for the sum of 250 thousand crowns. The par value in dollars at that time was $50,000. That mortgage of
850,000	in 1917 was paid in August of 1922 in full for S3.12L A pension before the war of 30 thousand crowns was equal to about $6,000. To-day that same pension would buy you a breakfast. In the middle of August $1 would buy about one thousand marks in Germany. In January of this year $1 would buy more than eight thousand marks. Now

France has marched into the Ruhr. The immediate result of that action was to reduce the value of the mark to the vanishing point. Between January 14 and 18, the mark de-' dined by 50 per cent. To-day you can buy 1 million marks for $50. The result of that invasion was the immediate rise in the cost of living and it at once doubled the difficulty of the payment of German reparations.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us look at the position that Germany is in with regard to its ability to meet the reparations. The total of the European debts to the United States of America is about $11,525,000,000. Of this England owes $4,747,000,000; France $3,770,000,000; and Italy owes $1,891,000,000. The remainder is owed by 17 other European nations. Now even should series C amounting to 82 billions of gold marks be cancelled, the remaining 50 billions of gold marks, or 12J- billion dollars is more than the total owed by 20 European nations to the United States. Now if these nations, which have already received more than a billion in gold and several billions in value in commodities are unable or have not-with one exception, the proud exception of Great Britain,-been able to pay even interest it appears to be reasonable to believe that Germany may be unable to pay any large part of the reparations amounting as they do to so much greater sums.
Force has failed. I personally do not think there is any possible prospect of success in the French invasion of the Ruhr district. We have seen in the last few days the collapse of industries in Germany, and we have seen strikes and other disturbances started, the outcome of which I am sure every member of this House dreads.
On one point I must agree with the last speaker. We must give every credit to Great Britain for the magnanimous position she took at the Paris conference, and I desire to remind the House of it. The offer was that Britain woud cancel France's debt to her. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to note that Britain proposed that she should cancel her debt to France, provided France would consent to a reduction of the German indemnity, and would drop altogether the proposition of bringing economic and military pressure to bear on Germany. I read that statement in the Montreal Gazette of 13th December, 1922.
Now, might we not follow England's example? I do not think the exact amount of reparation due to Canada has even been announced. It -must be a comparatively small amount, and it will make little difference to us. No computation has been made of what is due to us by Germany up to this time. If

German Reparations
we pass this resolution perhaps we may in some small degree help to eliminate the old hatreds that we see rising up, even around us in this House, and we may be able to assist European reconstruction. When we have a crippled horse, Mr. Speaker, we do not cripple it further. We put it in a stable, and take it out, and feed it, if we think it can recover. If we think it can be made to do any work in the future we feed it, nurse it and look after it. If we do not think so, then we shoot it and put it out of misery. If we could find out just exactly what Germany's capacity is, and decide once and for all whether she can pay or not pay, then we could either put her out of misery, as France appears to be prepared to do, or sacrifice our reparations.

subtopic: GERMAN REPARATIONS . MOTION BY MR. WOODSWORTH FOR WITHDRAWAL OF CANADA'S CLAIMS
speechtext: Before the hon. member finishes, will he tell us whether he is in favor of the resolution of the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg that Canada should withdraw all claims against Germany?

subtopic: GERMAN REPARATIONS . MOTION BY MR. WOODSWORTH FOR WITHDRAWAL OF CANADA'S CLAIMS
speechtext:
I would appeal to this House to support the resolution that Canada should withdraw all claims to reparations in the interest of European peace, in our own interest, if you want to come nearer home, and in the interest of agriculture, if you wish to come still closer home.
Let me suggest to hon. members that we are told to-day, when we protest against the price we are receiving for our grain, that the low price is due to the appalling conditions in central Europe. May I say also that I hope this House will, in the interest of humanity, in the essential interest of the economic reconstruction in Europe and of human welfare and peace, support this resolution.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Fort William and Rainy River):
subtopic: GERMAN REPARATIONS . MOTION BY MR. WOODSWORTH FOR WITHDRAWAL OF CANADA'S CLAIMS
speechtext:
I may say at the beginning of my remarks that I certainly cannot support the motion of the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth). It is true, Sir, that if things go as they seem to be going in Europe, it is very probable that this country will receive nothing in the shape' of reparations. And yet, if my memory serves me correctly, the revised amount of reparations which under the Peace Treaty was to be paid by Germany was thirty billion dollars. Originally almost double that amount was proposed. Suppose the last revised figures amount to thirty billions, then by Keynes' latest works which I have consulted to verify the facts, if that thirty billions were paid, Canada would receive one per cent, roughly, which means that Canada would get about three hundred million dollars, and yet my
hon. friend from Winnipeg, looking at it from a cold blooded business standpoint, suggests in a three line resolution that' we pass a motion in this House to forego that three hundred million dollars. It is doubtful if Canada will ever receive very much reparations, but there is another standpoint from which to view this question, and that is this: The passing of such a resolution in this House would help to complicate the already very much complicated conditions in Europe for by such a resolution you say once and for all that you do not believe that Germany has any right to pay you anything. By such action you condemn France, who has recently gone" into the Ruhr, and I may say here, though it has no special bearing on this subject, that I have very great sympathy with France in her action in going into the Ruhr. When you remember the conditions which France fwent through, the suffering which France endured when the Germans invaded that country in 1870, when you remember that at that time the German troops first went to Versailles, and imposed upon France the most humiliating terms of peace, and on top of that, a very heavy reparation, you can well understand and appreciate the feelings of the French people to-day. The reparation demanded then was considered very heavy. Considering the value of money at that time and the value of money at the present time, the reparation payment which Germany imposed on France on account of a war which only lasted about six months, was, I believe, nearly equivalent to the thirty billion dollars imposed upon Germany on account of the recent war, and when Germany imposed that payment on France, she stayed in France with her army until the money was paid. Therefore, I feel very sympathetic towards France in the action which she has taken at the present time.
However, laying that aside for a moment, I do not believe it is the duty of this country to be the first to complicate the already very difficult conditions which exist in Europe. That is my first reason for very strongly opposing this resolution. My hon. friend from Winnipeg mentioned the boys and girls of Germany,-and I do not say this with any desire to arouse passion-when he mentioned the boys and girls of Germany, one was forced to think of the boys and girls in this country whose fathers had died in order to bring about peace in the world. While I do not accuse him of doing this with this object in view the intention apparently was to let the little boys and girls in Canada
German Reparations

suffer so that the little boys and girls in Germany might be relieved of the pressure of debt which they would have to pay in the future. According to all the despatches that we read at the present time, while the conditions in Germany are very bad just at the moment because of the Ruhr invasion, yet up to recently they had been very good probably better than the conditions in any country in Europe at least, and perhaps even better than conditions in Canada. According to persons whom I have met, who have visited Germany within the last year or year and a half, there was practically no unemployment in Germany, and yet we have a large unemployment problem in this country. And certainly, so far as Great Britain and France are concerned, and particularly Great Britain, the unemployment situation is critical. Indeed, so severe is it in Great. Britain that the British parliament, according to a despatch in the press to-night, was this very*day debating the question whether they might solve the unemployment problem by getting the unemployed to emigrate. Now, when a condition is so critical in a country that the unemployed are asked to emigrate as the only solution of the difficulty, it is obvious that conditions generally must be very bad indeed. I have certainly never read any suggestion coming from Germany or any of its people that there are in that country such conditions of unemployment as would necessitate anyone emigrating .from Germany.
I do not intend to waste the time of the House going into all arguments put forth, because many of them have been dealt with very ably by my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens). But with reference to Mr. Keynes, I have never read any statement of his suggesting that there should be an entire abandonment of all reparation claims. Ha did suggest that the reparation claims originally imposed against Germany by the Allies at the Versailles conference were too severe and he said that they should be cut down. But so far as I can learn Mr. Keynes suggested something like thirty billion dollars as possibly an amount which Germany could pay. He may have proposed a lower sum, but there has not been anywhere in his writings any suggestion that the reparation claims should be wholly wiped out. It is true that some of the men quoted by the hon. member who intoduced the resolution have probably taken that attitude.
In considering the stand which some men even in the British Isles have taken in contradistinction to the position held by the people of France, we must bear in mind that the conditions are altogether different in the
.'Mr. Manion.]
two countries. In England we find a country that was dependent to a great extent on its trade in the days before the war, and much of that trade was with Germany. So that, looking at the matter absolutely from the materialistic standpoint, the British people would probably be glad, as most of us no doubt would be glad in the interests of the world at large, but the English people particularly would be glad, to see Germany rehabilitated in order that there might be a resumption of British trade with Germany and British industries be once again put on their feet. France, on the other hand, was not so great a trading nation as Great Britain. She is looking at the danger that threatens her northern and eastern border from a country which invaded her and Belgium in cold blood. France is looking to the future, and I certainly do not blame her for so doing.
I shall vote against this resolution and I shall certainly be disappointed if it receives any great support in this House. If you support it you are practically exonerating Germany from all blame for bringing on the war. And while I cannot work myself up into a passion of hatred against Germany, I for one shall not vote to exonerate her from responsibility for the war through which we passed. But not only would a vote for this resolution be exonerating Germany, it would appear to me to be a condemnation of the actions of this country, of France, of England, and of the United States, which quietly for a period of three years discussed the question before going into the war. It would be a condemnation of all our Allies; it would be a condemnation of our boys who went overseas and of those who died there. I do not think, therefore, that we should vote for any such resohition as this, and it would be a great disappointment to the people of this country if this House at the present time, in the present condition of our finances, in the present situation in Europe, should pass a resolution of'this character. For these reasons I shall emphatically oppose the resolution.
On motion of Mr. Warner, the debate was adjourned.
